label: expUnit
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{expUnit}
      Let $G= G_d(F)$ and $\pi$ be a representation of $G$, parabolically induced from a unitary supercuspidal representation. Then, for every parabolic subgroup $P$ of $G$, the exponents of $r_P^{G}(\pi)$ are all unitary.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every parabolic is supposed to be standard. Let $Q=MU_Q$ be a parabolic subgroup of $G_d(F)$ and $\sigma$ be a unitary supercuspidal representation of $M$, denote by $\omega_\sigma$ its central (unitary) character. We set $\pi=i_Q^G(\sigma)$. Recall that, due to the geometric lemma, for all parabolic subgroup $P=LU_P$ the representation $r_P^G(\pi)$ admits a filtration, with associated graded vector space, on which $L$ acts, is isomorphic to  
    $$\bigoplus_w i_{L\cap w^{-1}Q}^{L} (r^{M}_{M\cap wP} \sigma)^w$$
    where $w$ runs over representatives of the double cosets $Q\backslash G/P$. Since $\sigma$ is supercuspidal, the only $w$ that contribute to this direct sum are the ones that verify $M\subseteq wP $. In particular, we get that for all $w$, $Z_L\subseteq Z_{w^{-1}M} \cong Z_{M}$. Hence
    $$\bigoplus_w i_{L\cap w^{-1}Q}^{L} ( \sigma^w).$$
    the exponents of $r_P^G(\pi)$ are the central characters of the various $ i_{L\cap w^{-1}Q}^{L} ( \sigma^w)$, which are the restrictions to $Z_L$ of the central characters of $\sigma^w$, that are unitary by assumption.

label: asympW
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{asympW}
    Let $\pi$ be a generic representation of finite length of $G_n$. Then there exists $l\in \mathbb{N}$ such that any $W \in \mathcal{W}(\pi, \psi_n)$ can be written as 
    $$W(uak) = \psi_n(u) \sum_{B_n\subseteq Q}\delta^{1/2}_Q(a)\sum_{\mu \in \mathrm{Exp}_Q(\pi)} \phi_{Q, \mu}(a, k), \ a \in A_n, \ u \in N_n, k\in K_0$$
    where for all $k\in K_0$, $\phi_{Q, \mu}(\cdot, k)$ is a finite sum of functions of the form $\xi.\varphi$ where $\xi \in \mathcal{F}(A_n)_{\chi,l}$, with
    $$\mathcal{F}(A_n)_{\chi,l}=\{f: A \to \mathbb{C},  \ (R(a_1)-\chi(a_1))\cdots (R(a_l)-\chi(a_l))f=0, \ \forall a_1, \dots,a_l\in A\},$$
    and $\varphi$ is a smooth function with compact support on $F^{\Delta_0\backslash \Delta_0^Q}\times (F^\times)^{\Delta_0^Q}$, and $\phi_{Q, \mu}$ is invariant under a compact open subgroup of $K_0$. Note that for the function $\varphi$ we have identified $A_n/Z_n$ with $(F^\times)^{\Delta_0}$ through the application $a\mapsto (\alpha(a))_{\alpha\in \Delta_0}$, and $\Delta_0^Q$ is the set of simple roots of $A_n$ in $M_Q$.

title: Definition
body_md:
\label{RegInt}
    We say that $f\in C^\infty(N_n)$ admits a \emph{regularized integral}, if there exists a compact-open subgroup $K_1$ of $N_n$, such that for all compact-open subgroup $K_2$ of $N_n$ containing $K_1$, we have 
    $$\int_{K_1}f(u)du = \int_{K_2}f(u)du.$$
    In that case, we denote by 
    $$\int^*_{N_n} f(u)du = \int_{K_1}f(u)du$$
    the \emph{regularized integral} of $f$.

title: Definition
body_md:
A \emph{Langlands parameter} of $\mathbf{G}$ (or of $\mathbf{G}(F)$) is the $\mathbf{G}^\vee$-conjugacy class of a continuous homomorphism $\varphi : W_F'\to \ ^L\mathbf{G}$ such that 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item the restriction of $\varphi$ to $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ is algebraic, 
        \item $\varphi$ sends elements of $W_F$ to semi-simple elements,
        \item $\varphi$ commutes with the natural projections $W_F'\to W_F$ and $^L\mathbf{G}\to W_F$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Let $\Phi(\mathbf{G})$ be the set of Langlands parameters of $\mathbf{G}$.

    A Langlands parameter $\varphi$ is \emph{tempered}, if the projection of $\varphi(W_F)$ to $\mathbf{G}^\vee$ is bounded, and we denote by $\Phi_{\mathrm{temp}}(\mathbf{G})$ the set of such parameters. We say that $\varphi$ is \emph{discrete} if it is tempered and the centralizer of $\varphi(W'_F)$ in $\mathbf{G}^\vee$ is finite modulo $Z(\mathbf{G}^\vee)^{W_F}$ and the set of discrete Langlands parameter is denoted $\Phi_2(\mathbf{G})$.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $R$ be a representation of $W'_E$ (we also denote by $R$ the vector space associated to this representation), and $R^\rho$ be the conjugate representation with the same action of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$, and for $\tau\in W_E$, $R^\rho(\tau) =R( \rho\tau \rho^{-1})$. 

    The representation $R$ is \emph{conjugate-orthogonal}, if there is a non-degenerate bilinear form $B:R\times R \to \mathbb{C}$, which satisfies, 
    $$\left\{\begin{array}{cc}
         B(R(\tau) r , R(\rho\tau \rho^{-1})t) = B(r, t)  \\
         B(t, r) = B(r, R(\rho^2)t)
    \end{array} \right.,$$
    for all $\tau \in W_E'$.

    The representation $R$ is \emph{conjugate-symplectic}, if there is a non-degenerate bilinear form $B$ which satisfies
    $$\left\{\begin{array}{cc}
         B(R(\tau) r , R(\rho\tau \rho^{-1})t) = B(r, t)  \\
         B(t, r) = - B(r, R(\rho^2)t)
    \end{array} \right.,$$
    for all $\tau \in W_E'$.

    In both case, the form $B$ gives an isomorphism of representations
    $$f: R^\rho \to R^\vee,$$
    whose conjugate-dual
    $$(f^\vee)^\rho : R^\rho \to ((R^\rho)^\vee)^\rho \overset{\sim}{\rightarrow} R^\vee$$
    satisfies
    $$(f^\vee)^\rho = b.f$$
    where $b$ is the sign of $B$, i.e. $b=1$ in the conjugate-orthogonal case, $b=-1$ in the conjugate-symplectic case.

    We say that a representation is \emph{$(\pm1)$-conjugate-dual} when it is conjugate-orthogonal ($(1)$-conjugate-dual) or conjugate-symplectic ($(-1)$-conjugate-dual).

name: Conjugate-dual representations

title: Example
body_md:
Let $\varphi = \psi \boxtimes \mathrm{Sym}^{d-1}$ be an irreducible Langlands parameter for $\mathrm{GL}_n(E)$. The representation $\mathrm{Sym}^{d-1}$ is orthogonal when $d$ is odd, and symplectic when $d$ is even. Then, $\varphi$ is conjugate-orthogonal (resp. conjugate-symplectic) if $\psi$ is conjugate orthogonal and $d$ is odd (resp. even) or $\psi$ is conjugate-symplectic and $d$ is even (resp. odd).

    A conjugate-dual Langlands parameter $\varphi = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k \varphi_i$ can also have an irreducible component $\varphi_i$ that is neither conjugate orthogonal nor conjugate-symplectic but in that case, there exists $j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$ such that $\varphi_j \cong \varphi_i^*$.

label: LAd
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{LAd}
    Let $Q=MU$ be a standard parabolic subgroup of $G$, $\sigma$ be an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $M$, and $\pi = i_Q^{G}\sigma$. The representation $\pi$ is irreducible if and only if $L(s, \pi, \mathrm{Ad})$ has no pole at $s=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have $M=G_{n_1}(E)\times \cdots \times G_{n_k}(E)$ and $\pi = \sigma_1 \times \cdots \times \sigma_k$. Let $\mathrm{Frob}_E$ be a Frobenius of the Weil group $W_E$ of $E$, we have $W_E=\mathcal{I}_E \rtimes \langle \mathrm{Frob}_E\rangle$. If $\varphi_\pi$ is the Langlands parameter corresponding to $\pi$, we have
   $$\mathrm{Ad}\circ \varphi_\pi = \varphi_\pi \otimes \varphi_\pi^\vee,$$
   and 
   $$\varphi_\pi = \varphi_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus \varphi_k,$$
   where $\varphi_i$ is the Langlands parameter of $\sigma_i$, for all $i\in \{ 1, \dots, k \}$. Hence, 
   $$L(s, \pi, \mathrm{Ad}) = \prod_{1 \leq i, j \leq k }L(s, \varphi_i\otimes \varphi_j^\vee).$$
   The function $L(s, \pi, \mathrm{Ad})$ has a pole at $1$ if and only if there exists $i,j\in \{1, \dots , k\}$, $i\not = j$, such that 
   $$\mathrm{det}(1-q_E^{-1}\varphi_i\otimes \varphi_j^\vee (\mathrm{Frob}_E)\vert V^{\mathcal{I}_E})=0$$
   where $V$ denotes the vector space $V_i \otimes V_j^\vee$ of the representation $\varphi_i \otimes \varphi_j^\vee$. Recall that we have a $W'_E$-equivariant isomorphism
   $$\begin{array}{cccc}
        & V_i\otimes V_j^\vee & \longrightarrow & \mathrm{Hom}(V_j, V_i) \\
        & v_i\otimes v_j^\vee & \longmapsto & (w\in V_j \mapsto v_j^\vee(w)v_i)
   \end{array}$$
   As $q_E^{-1} = \vert \mathrm{Frob}_E \vert$ is an eigen value of $\varphi_i\otimes \varphi_j^\vee (\mathrm{Frob}_E)$ if and only if for some non-zero $v\in V^{\mathcal{I}_E}$ 
   $$\varphi_i \otimes \varphi_j^\vee (\mathrm{Frob}_E)v= q_E^{-1}v,$$
   we want to find the fixed points of the action of $W_E$ on $\mathrm{Hom}(V_j, \vert  \cdot  \vert_E V_i)$. These fixed points correspond to the intertwining operators between $\vert  \cdot  \vert_E \varphi_i$ and $\varphi_j$ (which are irreducible). Finally, $L(s, \pi, \mathrm{Ad})$ has a pole at $1$ if and only if there exist $i,j\in \{1, \dots , k\}$, $i\not = j$, such that  $\mathrm{Hom}_{W_E}(V_j, \vert  \cdot  \vert_E V_i) \not = 0$ or equivalently, such that $\sigma_j \cong \sigma_i \vert\det \vert_E$. Thanks to the irreducibility criterion of Bernstein-Zelevinsky \cite{BZ1} (Theorem 4.2), we conclude that $L(s, \pi, \mathrm{Ad})$ has no pole at $s=1$ if and only if $\pi$ is irreducible.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $V$ be a Hermitian space, and $U(V)$ be its associated unitary group. Let ${}^LU(V) = \mathrm{GL}(M)\rtimes W_F$. The L-group of $\mathrm{Res}_{E/F}(\mathrm{GL}(V))$ can be identified as
    $$H= (\mathrm{GL}(M) \times \mathrm{GL}(M)) \rtimes \mathrm{Gal}(E/F),$$
    where $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)\cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ acts by permuting the two factors of $\mathrm{GL}(M)$. Let $H_0 = \mathrm{GL}(M) \times \mathrm{GL}(M)$, we have 
    $$\mathrm{Ind}_{H^0}^H(M \boxtimes M) = \mathrm{As}^+(M) \oplus \mathrm{As}^-(M)$$
    where $\mathrm{As}^+(M)$ is the space $M \boxtimes M$ on which $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$ acts by permuting the two copies of $M$, and $\mathrm{As}^-(M)$ is obtained by twisting $\mathrm{As}^+(M)$ by the non trivial character of $H/H_0$.

label: ZBeta
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{ZBeta}
    Let $\pi \in \mathrm{Temp}_{G_n(F)}(G_n(E))$. For all $W\in \mathcal{W}(\pi, \psi_n)$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(F^n)$, 
    $$Z(1, W, \phi)=\hat{\phi}(0)\beta(W), $$
    up to a constant that depends on the choices of the measures on $N_n(F) \backslash G_n(F)$ and $N_n(F)\backslash P_n(F)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\pi \in \mathrm{Temp}_{G_n(F)}(G_n(E))$. First of all, recall that the restriction of $\beta$ to $\mathcal{W}(\pi, \psi_n)$ is $G_n(F)$-invariant (see Section 4 of \cite{Offen}). Let $W\in \mathcal{W}(\pi, \psi_n)$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(F^n)$, we have 
    \begin{align*}
         Z(1,W, \phi) &= \int_{P_n(F)\backslash G_n(F)} \int_{N_n(F)\backslash P_n(F)} W(ph) \phi(e_nph) \vert \det ph \vert \vert \det p \vert^{-1} dp dh, \\
        & = \int_{N_n(F)\backslash P_n(F)} W(p) dp \int_{P_n(F)\backslash G_n(F)} \phi(e_nh) \vert \det h \vert dh.
    \end{align*}
    Setting $x=e_nh\in F^n$, we get 
    $$Z(1,W, \phi)= \beta(W) \int_{F^n}\phi(x)dx = \hat{\phi}(0) \beta(W).$$

label: propcuspBC
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us recall that any irreducible representation of $W_E'$ is of the form $\Tilde{\psi}\boxtimes \mathrm{Sym}^{d-1}$, with $\Tilde{\psi}$ an irreducible representation of $W_E$ and $\mathrm{Sym}^{d-1}$ is the irreducible representation of dimension $d$ of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$. Hence, the semi-simplification is of the form
    $$\bigoplus_{i=0}^{d-1}\Tilde{\psi}\vert \cdot \vert^{\frac{d-(2i+1)}{2}}.$$
                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                      
    
    Let $\psi: W_E \to \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be a conjugate-orthogonal representation. Denote by $\mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)$ the set of isomorphism classes of irreducible and unitary representations of $W_E$. Then $\psi$ can be decomposed in the form
    $$\psi=\bigoplus_{\psi'\in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)}\bigoplus_{a\in E_{\psi'}} \psi'\vert \cdot \vert^ a,$$
    where each $E_{\psi'}\subset \mathbb{R}$ is a multiset. For $a, b\in \mathbb{R}$, such that $b-a\in \mathbb{N}$, we define the Weil-Deligne representation
    $$[a,b] := \vert \cdot\vert^{\frac{a+b}{2}}\boxtimes \mathrm{Sym}^{b-a},$$
    and from now on every segment $[a, b]= \{a, a+1, \dots, b\}$ is identified with this Weil-Deligne representation. We let $l([a,b])=b-a$ the \emph{length} of the segment $[a,b]$. When $a=-b$, the corresponding Weil-Deligne representation $ \mathrm{Sym}^{2b}$ is self-dual, of \emph{sign} $\mathrm{sgn}([-b,b])=(-1)^{2b}$.
    
    Let $\varphi$ be a semi-simple representation of $W_E'$. There exists a unique family $(S_{\Tilde{\psi}})_{\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)}$ of multisets of segments such that
    $$\varphi \cong \bigoplus_{\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)} \bigoplus_{I \in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi} \otimes I.$$
    Moreover $\varphi$ is conjugate-orthogonal (or $\mathrm{sgn}(\varphi)=1$), if and only if it satisfies the following conditions:  
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] For every multiset $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, we have 
        $$S_{\Tilde{\psi}^*} = -S_{\Tilde{\psi}},$$
        where $-S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ is the multiset $\{[-b, -a], \ [a,b]\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}\}$.
        \item[(ii)] \begin{itemize}
            \item If ${\Tilde{\psi}}$ is conjugate-orthogonal, then any symmetric segment $I=-I$ such that $\mathrm{sgn}(I)=-1$ appears with even multiplicity in $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$.
            \item If ${\Tilde{\psi}}$ is conjugate-symplectic, then any symmetric segment $I=-I$ such that $\mathrm{sgn}(I)=1$ appears with even multiplicity in $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$.
        \end{itemize} 
    \end{enumerate}
    Moreover, we have the decomposition
    \begin{align*}
        L(s, \varphi, \mathrm{As}^-) &= \prod_{\Tilde{\psi}} \prod_{I \in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}} L(s,  \Tilde{\psi} \otimes I, \mathrm{As}^-) \prod_{\Tilde{\psi} \not \cong\Tilde{\psi}'}\prod_{I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}, \ J \in S_{\Tilde{\psi}'}} L(s, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I \otimes (\Tilde{\psi}')^c\otimes J) \\
        & \times \prod_{\Tilde{\psi}}\prod_{I\in \underset{I \in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}, \ J \in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}\backslash \{I\}}{\{I,J\} \subset S_{\Tilde{\psi}}}} L(s, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I_i \otimes \Tilde{\psi}^c\otimes I_j)
    \end{align*}
    
    From there, we see that $L(s, \varphi, \mathrm{As}^-)$ has a pole at $s=1$ if and only if there exist $\Tilde{\psi} \in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)$ and $I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ such that $L(s, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I, \mathrm{As}^-)$ has a pole at $s=1$, or there exist $\Tilde{\psi}, \Tilde{\psi}'\in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)$ and $I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}, \ J \in S_{\Tilde{\psi}'}$ such that $L(s, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I \otimes (\Tilde{\psi}')^c\otimes J)$ has a pole at $s=1$.
    
    Let $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)$ and let $I=[a,b] \subset \mathbb{R}$. Denote $$\Tilde{\psi}_I= \Tilde{\psi} \otimes I = \Tilde{\psi} \vert  \cdot \vert ^{\frac{a+b}{2}}\boxtimes \mathrm{Sym}^{b-a},$$
    and $V_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, $V_{b-a}$, the vector space on which $W_E$ acts by $\Tilde{\psi} \vert\cdot \vert^{\frac{a+b}{2}}$ and $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ by $\mathrm{Sym}^{b-a}$ respectively.
    \begin{lem}
        For all $s \in \mathbb{C}$, all $\tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)$ and all segment $I=[a,b]\subset \mathbb{R}$, we have 
        $$L(s, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I, \mathrm{As}^-) = \prod_{m=0}^{b-a} L(s+2b-m, \Tilde{\psi},\mathrm{As}^{(-1)^{m+1}}).$$
    \end{lem}
    
    \begin{proof}
    Recall that the representation $\mathrm{As}^-(\Tilde{\psi}_I)$ is realized on $V_{\Tilde{\psi}}\otimes V_{\Tilde{\psi}}\otimes V_{b-a}\otimes V_{b-a}$. For a certain $\sigma\in W_F\backslash W_E$,
    $$\mathrm{As}^-(\psi_I)(\sigma) = -((\mathrm{Id} \otimes \Tilde{\psi}(\sigma^2))\circ \iota_{V_{\Tilde{\psi}}}) \otimes \iota_{V_{b-a}}$$
    where $\iota_V(v_1\otimes v_2)=v_2\otimes v_1$, for $v_1,v_2\in V$. For all $\tau\in W_E$, $g\in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$
    $$\mathrm{As}^-(\Tilde{\psi}_I)(\tau, g) = (\Tilde{\psi}(\tau)\vert\tau\vert^{\frac{a+b}{2}}\otimes \Tilde{\psi}(\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1})\vert\tau\vert^{\frac{a+b}{2}})\otimes(\mathrm{Sym}^{b-a}(g)\otimes \mathrm{Sym}^{b-a}(g)).$$
    We have $V_{b-a}\otimes V_{b-a}\cong V_{2b-2a}\oplus V_{2b-2a-2} \oplus \cdots \oplus V_0$ (see p.87 in \cite{BroDi}) and $\iota_{V_{b-a}}$ is an involutive self-intertwining operator of this $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C)}$-representation, hence it acts by $\pm 1$ on each of the $V_{2i}$'s. More precisely, 
    \begin{lem}
        With the same notation, for all $i \in \{0, \dots, b-a\}$,
        $$\iota_{V_{b-a}}\vert_{V_{2i}} = (-1)^{b-a+i}\mathrm{Id}_{V_{2i}}.$$
    \end{lem}
    
    \begin{proof}
        $$\iota_{V_{b-a}} \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})}\left(\bigoplus_{i=0}^{b-a}V_{2i}, \bigoplus_{i=0}^{b-a}V_{2i} \right).$$
    As $V_{2i}$ is irreducible for all $i\in \{0, \dots b-a\}$, we therefore have 
    $$\iota_{V_{b-a}} \in \bigoplus_{i=0}^{b-a}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})}(V_{2i}, V_{2i}),$$
    which means that $\iota_{V_{b-a}}\vert_{V_{2i}} = \lambda_i \mathrm{Id}_{V_{2i}}$ is a homothety such that $\lambda_i^2=1$ because 
    $$\iota_{V_{b-a}} \circ \iota_{V_{b-a}} = \mathrm{Id}_{V_{b-a}}.$$
    Recall that 
    $$V_{b-a} \otimes V_{b-a} = \mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a}) \oplus \Lambda^2(V_{b-a}), $$
    where $\Lambda^2(V_{b-a})$ denotes the exterior square of $\Lambda^2(V_{b-a})$. By definition, $\iota_{V_{b-a}}$ acts by $+1$ on $\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a})$ and by $-1$ on $\Lambda^2(V_{b-a})$.
    Following \cite{FultonHarris}, 11.1, we show that for all integer $n$
    $$\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{n}) = \bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} V_{2n-4i}.$$
    The weights of $V_{n}$ are $n, n-2, \dots, -n+2, -n$, hence the weights of $V_n \otimes V_n$ are of the form 
    $$\alpha +\beta , \ \text{with} \ \alpha, \beta \in \{n, n-2, \dots, -n+2, -n\},$$
    we can arrange them in a matrix as follows
    $$E := \begin{pmatrix}
        2n & 2n-2 & 2n-4 & \cdots & 0 \\
        2n-2 & 2n-4 & 2n-6 & \cdots & -2 \\
        2n-4 & 2n-6 & 2n-8 &  \cdots & -4 \\
        \vdots & \vdots &  & \ddots &  \vdots \\
        0 & -2 & -4 & \cdots & -2n
    \end{pmatrix}$$
    and remark that the weights of $\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a})$ are given by the upper triangular matrix
    $$\begin{pmatrix}
        2n & 2n-2 & 2n-4 & \cdots & 0 \\
        * & 2n-4 & 2n-6 & \cdots & -2 \\
        * & * & 2n-8 &  \cdots & -4 \\
        \vdots & \vdots &  & \ddots &  \vdots \\
        * & * & * & \cdots & -2n
    \end{pmatrix}.$$
    As the representations are entirely determined by their eigenvalues, we can identify the irreducible components of $\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a})$. Namely, the first line of $E$ together with the last column give 
    $$2n, 2n-2, \dots, -2n$$
    as eigenvalues, corresponding to $V_{2n}$. We then take the second line and the $(n-1)$-th column and obtain $V_{2n-4}$. We iterate this step until the $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$-th line and column. This shows the formula 
    $$\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{n}) \cong \bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} V_{2n-4i}.$$
    We deduce from that that for all $i \in \{0, \dots, b-a\}$,
    $$\iota_{V_{b-a}}\vert_{V_{2i}} = (-1)^{b-a+i}\mathrm{Id}_{V_{2i}}.$$
    
    \end{proof}

    Finally, we have 
    $$V_{\Tilde{\psi}}\otimes V_{\Tilde{\psi}}\otimes V_{b-a}\otimes V_{b-a} \cong \bigoplus_{m=0}^{b-a}(V_{\Tilde{\psi}}\otimes V_{\Tilde{\psi}})\otimes V_{2b-2a-2m}$$
    and 
    $$\mathrm{As}^-(\Tilde{\psi}_I) \cong \bigoplus_{m=0}^{b-a}\mathrm{As}^{(-1)^{m+1}}(\Tilde{\psi} \vert \cdot\vert^{\frac{a+b}{2}})\otimes \mathrm{Sym}^{2b-2a-2m}.$$
    In terms of segments, it becomes
    $$\mathrm{As}^-(\Tilde{\psi}_I) \cong \bigoplus_{m=0}^{b-a}\mathrm{As}^{(-1)^{m+1}}(\Tilde{\psi})\otimes [2a+m, 2b-m].$$
    Hence, 
    $$L(s, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I, \mathrm{As}^-) = \prod_{m=0}^{b-a} L(s+2b-m, \Tilde{\psi},\mathrm{As}^{(-1)^{m+1}}).$$
    \end{proof}
    
    Using this formula, we obtain that $L(s, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I, \mathrm{As}^-)$ has a pole at $s=1$ if and only if $-1-b \in \{a, a+1, \dots, b\}$ and $\Tilde{\psi}$ is $(-1)^{2b}$-conjugate-dual (with $(-1)$-conjugate-dual being conjugate-symplectic, and $1$ -conjugate-dual being conjugate-orthogonal). For the other L-factors, let $\Tilde{\psi}, \Tilde{\psi}'$ be irreducible and unitary Weil representations and $I=[a,b], \ J=[\alpha,\beta]$ two segments in $\mathbb{R}$. Then
    $$\Tilde{\psi} \otimes I \otimes (\Tilde{\psi'})^c \otimes J \cong \Tilde{\psi} \otimes (\Tilde{\psi'})^c \otimes \bigoplus_{m=0}^{\min(b-a, \beta-\alpha)}\left[a+\alpha+m, b+\beta-m\right].$$
    Therefore, 
    $$L(s,\Tilde{\psi} \otimes I \otimes (\Tilde{\psi'})^c \otimes J) = \prod_{m=0}^{\min(b-a, \beta-\alpha)} L(s+b+\beta-m,\Tilde{\psi} \otimes (\Tilde{\psi'})^c )$$
    has a pole at $s=1$ if and only if $ 1+b+\beta \in \{0, 1, \dots, \min( b-a, \beta-\alpha)\}$ and $\Tilde{\psi}^*\cong \Tilde{\psi'}$. Recall that two segments $[a, b]$ and $[\alpha, \beta]$ are said to be \emph{linked} if their union is still a segment and none of them is included in the other, when $a\leq \alpha$, i.e. $[a, b]$ is on the left of $[\alpha, \beta]$, we then write $[a, b]\prec[\alpha, \beta]$. With this notation, the condition 
    $$1+b+\beta \in \{0, 1, \dots, \min( b-a, \beta-\alpha)\}$$
    is equivalent to 
    $$I\prec -J, \ \ \mathrm{if} \ \  l(I)\leq l(J),$$
    and $J \prec -I$ otherwise.
    
    Let us reformulate our proposition in terms of segments. We know that
    $$\psi=\bigoplus_{\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u({W_E})}\bigoplus_{a\in E_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi}\vert \cdot \vert^ a.$$
    We want to show that there exists a unique partition $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ of $E_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ into segments, for all $\Tilde{\psi}$ such that
    $$\varphi = \bigoplus_{\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u({W_E})}\bigoplus_{I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi} \otimes I$$
    satisfies the following conditions.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\varphi^{ss}=\psi$, meaning that for all $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u({W_E})$, $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ is a partition of $E_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, in other words $\underset{I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}}{\bigsqcup}I = E_{\Tilde{\psi}}.$
        \item $\varphi$ is conjugate-orthogonal, that is:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item For all $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u({W_E})$, $S_{\Tilde{\psi}^*}=-S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, where $-S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ is the multiset $\{[-b, -a], \ [a,b]\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}\}$.
            \item For all $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u({W_E})$ and all $I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, if $\Tilde{\psi}^*\cong\Tilde{\psi}$, $I=-I$ and $\mathrm{sgn}(\Tilde{\psi})\mathrm{sgn}(I)=-1$, then $I$ appears with even multiplicity in $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$.
        \end{enumerate}
        \item For all $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u({W_E})$, all $I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ and all $J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}^*}$, if $l(I)\leq l(J)$ and $I\prec -J$, then $\Tilde{\psi}\cong \Tilde{\psi}^*$, $I=J$ and $I$ appears with multiplicity one in $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$.
        \item For all $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u({W_E})$ and all $I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, if $\Tilde{\psi} \cong \Tilde{\psi}^*$ and $I\prec -I$ then $\mathrm{sgn(\Tilde{\psi})}\mathrm{sgn}(I\cup-I)=-1$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Assuming the first conditions, conditions 3 and 4 are equivalent to : for all $\Tilde{\psi}$, and all $I,J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, if $I$ and $J$ are linked then  $\Tilde{\psi}^*\cong\Tilde{\psi}$, $J=-I$, $I$ appears with multiplicity one in $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ and $\mathrm{sgn(\Tilde{\psi})}\mathrm{sgn}(I\cup-I)=-1$.

    \begin{lem}[Decomposition in maximal segments]
        Let $E \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a finite multiset. Then, there exists a unique partition of $E$ into segments, 
        $$E = I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d,$$
        such that none of the segments $I_i$ are linked.
            
    \end{lem}
    
    \begin{proof}
        Let $x=\max(E)$, and take $y$ such that $[y, x] \subset E $ is maximal for this property. Set $E'=E\backslash [y, x]$, by induction $E'$ admits a unique partition $E'=I'_1\cup \cdots \cup I'_d$ such that none of the segments are linked. As $E=E'\cup [y, x]$, we have to show that for all $i\in \{1, \dots, d\}$, $I'_i$ is not linked to $[y, x]$. Suppose that there exists $i\in \{1, \dots, d\}$, such that $I'_i$ is linked to $[y, x]$, therefore there exists $z\in I'_i$, such that $z<y$ and $[z, x]\subset E$. But then $[z, x]$ is longer than $[y, x]$, which is not possible by assumption on $y$. Hence, the partition $E=I'_1\cup \cdots \cup I'_d\cup [y, x]$ works. To show the uniqueness of this decomposition, suppose that $E=I_1\cup \cdots\cup I_d$ is such that none of the $I_i$'s are linked and for all $i\in\{1, \dots, d\}$, $I_i \not = [y, x]$. Hence, there exist $i\not = j$ such that $y\in I_i$ and $x\in I_j$. As $E$ contains all the integers between $y$ and $x$, there exists $n\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $y+n \in I_i$ and $y+n+1\not \in I_i$ that is $y+n+1\in I_k$ with $k\not = i$. Then the segments $I_i$ and $I_k$ are linked, which contradicts the assumption on the $I_i$'s.
    \end{proof} 

    If $E_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ is the underlying multiset of a non conjugate-dual component $\Tilde{\psi}$, we apply the lemma to $E_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ and denote $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ the multiset of segments $I_i$ such that 
    $$E_{\Tilde{\psi}}=I_1\cup \cdots\cup I_d,$$
    where any two segments $I_i$, $I_j$ of $E_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ are not linked. We construct
    $$\varphi_{\Tilde{\psi}} = \bigoplus_{I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I,$$
    a component of $\varphi$ corresponding to $\Tilde{\psi}$. By assumption, the direct sum 
    $$\bigoplus_{a\in -E_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi}^*\vert \cdot \vert^a$$
    must appear in the decomposition of $\psi$, hence
    $$\varphi_{\Tilde{\psi}}^* =\varphi_{\Tilde{\psi}^*}= \bigoplus_{I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi}^{*} \otimes (-I)$$
    also appears in $\varphi$. In that case, the only L-factor that can have a pole at $s=1$ is 
    $$L(s, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I \otimes \Tilde{\psi}^\vee \otimes -J )$$
    with $I,J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$. This L-factor has a pole if and only if $I$ and $J$ are linked, but $J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ and the decomposition in maximal segments implies that $I$ and $J$ are not linked.

    \begin{lem}
        Let $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)$ be conjugate-dual and let $E=E_{\Tilde{\psi}} \subset \mathbb{R}$ be the corresponding multiset. Then, there exists a unique partition $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ of $E$ into segments such that:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}=-S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, 
            \item For all $I\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, if $I=-I$ and $\mathrm{sgn}(\Tilde{\psi})\mathrm{sgn}(I)=-1$, then $I$ appears with even multiplicity in $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$.
            \item For all $I,J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, if $I$ and $J$ are linked then $J=-I$, $I$ appears with multiplicity one in $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ and $\mathrm{sgn(\Tilde{\psi})}\mathrm{sgn}(I\cup-I)=-1$.           
        \end{enumerate}
    
    \end{lem}

    \begin{proof}
        Let $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)$ be conjugate-dual, that is $\Tilde{\psi}\cong \Tilde{\psi}^*$ and therefore $E=-E$. We prove the existence and unicity of such a partition of $E$ by induction. Let $x=\max(E)$, and take $y\in E$ such that $[ y, x ] \subset E$ and $[ y,x ] $ is of maximal length. Then, there are two possibilities, either $y\not = -x$ or $y =-x$.
        \begin{itemize}
            \item  If $y\not = -x$, then by symmetry $[-x, -y]\subset E$ and the segments $[-x, -y]$ and $[ y, x ]$ are not linked. Indeed, if they were linked, then $[ -x, -y ] \cup [ y, x ] =[ -x, -x ] \subset E$, which is impossible by hypothesis. Set $E' = E\backslash ([ -x, -y ]\cup [ y, x ])$, we have $E'=-E'$. Suppose by induction that $E'$ admits a unique decomposition $E'=I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d$ satisfying all the properties of the lemma, and denote by $S'$ this partition. Then $S = S'\cup \{[ -x, -y ], [ y, x ]\} $ is a partition of $E$, it follows directly that the first property is preserved for $S$. The second property is given by the fact that all the symmetric segments of the partition $S$ are in $S'$. It remains to show that $[ y, x ]$ is not linked to a $I_i$, for any $i\in\{1, \dots, d\}$ (it will imply also that $[ -x,-y]$ is not linked to any other segment in the decomposition). Assume that there exists $i\in \{1, \dots d\}$ such that $I_i$ is linked to $[ y,x]$, then $y-1\in I_i$ because $x=\max(E)$. But then $[ y-1, x] \subset E$ and its length is superior to the length of $[ y, x]$, which is not possible. Hence property 3 is also satisfied, because the only linked segments involved in the decomposition of $E$ are the ones inherited from $E'$. 
            
            Let us now prove the unicity. Suppose we have a partition $S_{\tilde{\psi}}$ of $E$ satisfying conditions 1, 2 and 3. To prove the unicity of $S_{\tilde{\psi}}$, it suffices to show, by induction again, that $ [x,y] \in S_{\tilde{\psi}}$. Let $I\in S_{\tilde{\psi}}$ containing $x$ and of maximal length. We have $\max I= x$ by assumption, and we can assume that $y = \min I-1$. As $[y,x] \subset E$, there exists $J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, such that $y\in J$, meaning that $I$ and $J$ are linked. By property 3, $J=-I$ so $-x \in J$ and the union of $I$ and $J$ is $[ -x, x ]$, which is not possible by assumption on $y$. That proves that $I=[ y,x]$, therefore the decomposition is unique.

            \item Assume now that $y=-x$, and $\Tilde{\psi}$ is conjugate-symplectic, i.e. $\mathrm{sgn}(\tilde{\psi})=-1$ which implies that $0$ has even multiplicity in $E$. We denote $m>0$ the largest integer such that $E$ contains all the elements of $[ -x, x ]$ with multiplicity at least $m$, and define $m[ -x,x] = [ -x,x] \sqcup \cdots \sqcup [ -x,x] $. 
            
            We have $\mathrm{sgn}[ -x,x]=1$, unless $x\in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}\backslash \mathbb{Z}$. Suppose $x\in \mathbb{Z}$, then $0\in[ -x,x]$. If the multiplicity $m$ of $[ -x,x]$ is odd, then there exists $z < x$ such that 
            $$[ -z,z]\subset E\backslash(m[ -x,x]),$$
            because $0$ has even multiplicity in $E$, and we take $z$ maximal for this property. Now set 
            $$E'=E\backslash ((m-1)[ -x,x]\sqcup[ -x,z]\sqcup [ -z,x]).$$
            We have $E'=-E'$ and the multiplicity of $0$ is still even. Suppose by induction, that $E'$ admits a unique decomposition $E'=I_1\sqcup \cdots \sqcup I_d$ satisfying all the properties of the lemma. Then the partition of $E$
            $$S_{\Tilde{\psi}}=\{I_1, \dots, I_d,(m-1)[ -x,x],[ -x,z],[ -z,x]\}$$
            automatically verifies properties 1 and 2. Note that if there exists $i\in \{1, \dots, d\}$ such that $I_i$ is linked to $[ -z, x]$ then either there exists an element $t\in I_i$ such that $t>x$ which is impossible, or there exists $t\in I_i$ such that $t<-z$ but in that case $-t>z$ which means that the segment $[ -t, t] \subset E\backslash(m[-x,x])$ is longer than $[ -z, z]$ and it is also impossible. If there exists $k\in \{1, \dots, d\}$ such that $I_k=[ -z,x]$ then $-I_k=[ -x,z]$ also appears but then $(m+1)[ -x,x]\subset E$ which is not possible by definition of $m$. This implies in particular that the third condition is still verified. Hence, the partition $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ satisfies all the conditions. 
            
            If $\mathrm{sgn}([ -x,x])=-1$, i.e. $x\in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}\backslash \mathbb{Z}$, then $0\not \in [ -x,x]$. We set 
            $$E'= E\backslash[ -x, x ]$$
            and decompose it as 
            $$E'=I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d$$
            satisfying all properties by induction. As $[-x,x]$ contains all the $I_i$ by assumption, it follows directly that $E = I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d \cup [-x,x]$ is a partition satisfying our conditions. 

            It remains to show that the partition $S_{\tilde{\psi}}$ given by the above algorithm is the unique one satisfying conditions 1, 2 and 3. Suppose that $E = I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d$ is another decomposition such that properties 1, 2 and 3 are satisfied. Let $I_i = [ y, x]$ be a segment containing $x$. We show that $I_i\in S_{\tilde{\psi}}$, i.e. that either  $y=-x$ and the multiplicity $m_i$ of $I_i$ is even, or $y=-z$, where $[-z,z]$ is maximal in $E\backslash (m[-x,x])$, with $m_i=1$. Recall that here, we have $[-x,x]\subset E$. In that case, either $I_i =-I_i$, or $I_i$ and $-I_i$ are linked because there exists a segment $I_k$ containing $y-1$, hence linked to $I_i$ and property 3 says that $I_k=-I_i$. Thanks to the second property, if $I_i=-I_i$, i.e. $y=-x$, then $m_i$ is even. If $I_i$ is linked to $-I_i$ then by the definition of $z$ there exists a segment $I_k$ containing $z$, and $-z\leq y \leq z<x$, forcing $I_k$ to be linked with $I_i$. Using the third property we have $I_k=-I_i$, hence $-z=y$, and $m_i=1$. Therefore, $I_i\in S_{\tilde{\psi}}$, the partition $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ is unique.

            \item Assume that $y=-x$, and $\tilde{\psi}$ is conjugate-orthogonal, i.e. $\mathrm{sgn}(\tilde{\psi})=1$. 
            
            If $\mathrm{sgn}[-x,x]=-1$, then $x\in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}\backslash\mathbb{Z}$. Suppose $[-x,x]$ appears with odd multiplicity $m$. If there exists $z \in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}\backslash \mathbb{Z}, \  z<x$ such that 
            $$[ -z, z] \subset E\backslash m[-x, x],$$ 
            we take $z$ maximal for this property. Then we set 
            $$E' = E\backslash ((m-1)[ -x,x] \cup [ -x,z]\cup [ -z,x])$$
            and suppose by induction that $E'$ admits a partition satisfying properties 1, 2 and 3, $E' = I_1 \cup\cdots \cup I_d $. We have 
            $$E= I_1 \cup\cdots \cup I_d \cup (m-1)[ -x,x] \cup [ -x,z]\cup [ -z,x]$$
            satisfying automatically properties 1 and 2. If there exists $i\in \{1, \dots, d\}$ such that $I_i$ is linked to $[ -z, x]$ then either there exists an element $t\in I_i$ such that $t>x$ which is impossible, or there exists $t\in I_i$ such that $t<-z$ but in that case $-t>z$ which means that the segment $[ -t, t] \subset E$ is longer than $[ -z, z]$ and it is also impossible. If, there exists $k\in \{1, \dots, d\}$ such that $I_k=[ -z,x]$ then $-I_k=[ -x,z]$ also appears but then $(m+1)[ -x,x]\subset E$ which is not possible by definition of $m$. This implies in particular that the third condition is still verified. Hence, the partition $$S_{\Tilde{\psi}}=\{I_1,\dots, I_d, (m-1)[ -x,x],[ -x,z], [ -z,x]\}$$
            satisfies all the conditions. If such an element $z$ does not exists in $E$, then we set 
            $$E'=E\backslash ((m-1)[ -x,x]\cup[ -x,-\frac{1}{2}]\cup [ \frac{1}{2},x]).$$ 
            The induction works in the same way.

             If $[ -x,x]$ is of odd length, then we set $E'= E\backslash[ -x, x ]$ and decompose it as $E'=I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d$ satisfying properties 1, 2, and 3, by induction. As $[-x,x]$ contains all the $I_i$ by assumption, it follows directly that $E = I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d \cup [-x,x]$ is a partition satisfying our conditions. 

             The proof of the unicity of the partition is the same as in the case of $\Tilde{\psi}$ conjugate-symplectic.

        \end{itemize}
    
        \end{proof}
    Once we have these partitions $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ for all $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)$ appearing in the decomposition of $\psi$, denote $\mathcal{C}$ the set of $\Tilde{\psi}$ that are conjugate-dual, and $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ the set of those that are not conjugate-dual. We set 

    $$\varphi = \bigoplus_{\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathcal{C}} \bigoplus_{I \in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi} \otimes I\bigoplus_{\Tilde{\psi} \in \overline{\mathcal{C}}}\bigoplus_{J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi}\otimes J.$$
    As $\psi$ is conjugate-orthogonal, for all $\Tilde{\psi} \in \overline{\mathcal{C}}$, we also have $\Tilde{\psi}^* \in \overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and $S_{\tilde{\psi}^*}=-S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, this implies that 
    $$\bigoplus_{\Tilde{\psi} \in \overline{\mathcal{C}}}\bigoplus_{J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi}\otimes J$$
    is conjugate-orthogonal. Moreover, for all $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathcal{C}$, conditions 1 and 2 of the above lemma ensure that
    $$ \bigoplus_{I \in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi} \otimes I$$
    is conjugate-orthogonal. Therefore $\varphi$ is indeed conjugate-orthogonal. The third condition of lemma is equivalent to the fact that for all $\Tilde{\psi} \in \mathcal{C}$ 
    $$L(s, \bigoplus_{I \in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}} \Tilde{\psi} \otimes I, \mathrm{As}^-),  \ \mathrm{and} \ L(s, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I \otimes \Tilde{\psi}^\vee \otimes J )$$
    with $I,J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, have no pole at $s=1$. We have already seen that for all $\Tilde{\psi}\in \overline{\mathcal{C}}$, the only L-factor that can have a pole is
    $$L(1, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I \otimes \Tilde{\psi}^\vee \otimes -J )$$
    with $I,J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$. This does not happen because of the partition in maximal segments. Finally, this Langlands' parameter $\varphi$ is unique thanks to the uniqueness of $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ for all $\Tilde{\psi}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the representation $\mathrm{As}^-(\Tilde{\psi}_I)$ is realized on $V_{\Tilde{\psi}}\otimes V_{\Tilde{\psi}}\otimes V_{b-a}\otimes V_{b-a}$. For a certain $\sigma\in W_F\backslash W_E$,
    $$\mathrm{As}^-(\psi_I)(\sigma) = -((\mathrm{Id} \otimes \Tilde{\psi}(\sigma^2))\circ \iota_{V_{\Tilde{\psi}}}) \otimes \iota_{V_{b-a}}$$
    where $\iota_V(v_1\otimes v_2)=v_2\otimes v_1$, for $v_1,v_2\in V$. For all $\tau\in W_E$, $g\in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$
    $$\mathrm{As}^-(\Tilde{\psi}_I)(\tau, g) = (\Tilde{\psi}(\tau)\vert\tau\vert^{\frac{a+b}{2}}\otimes \Tilde{\psi}(\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1})\vert\tau\vert^{\frac{a+b}{2}})\otimes(\mathrm{Sym}^{b-a}(g)\otimes \mathrm{Sym}^{b-a}(g)).$$
    We have $V_{b-a}\otimes V_{b-a}\cong V_{2b-2a}\oplus V_{2b-2a-2} \oplus \cdots \oplus V_0$ (see p.87 in \cite{BroDi}) and $\iota_{V_{b-a}}$ is an involutive self-intertwining operator of this $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C)}$-representation, hence it acts by $\pm 1$ on each of the $V_{2i}$'s. More precisely, 
    \begin{lem}
        With the same notation, for all $i \in \{0, \dots, b-a\}$,
        $$\iota_{V_{b-a}}\vert_{V_{2i}} = (-1)^{b-a+i}\mathrm{Id}_{V_{2i}}.$$
    \end{lem}
    
    \begin{proof}
        $$\iota_{V_{b-a}} \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})}\left(\bigoplus_{i=0}^{b-a}V_{2i}, \bigoplus_{i=0}^{b-a}V_{2i} \right).$$
    As $V_{2i}$ is irreducible for all $i\in \{0, \dots b-a\}$, we therefore have 
    $$\iota_{V_{b-a}} \in \bigoplus_{i=0}^{b-a}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})}(V_{2i}, V_{2i}),$$
    which means that $\iota_{V_{b-a}}\vert_{V_{2i}} = \lambda_i \mathrm{Id}_{V_{2i}}$ is a homothety such that $\lambda_i^2=1$ because 
    $$\iota_{V_{b-a}} \circ \iota_{V_{b-a}} = \mathrm{Id}_{V_{b-a}}.$$
    Recall that 
    $$V_{b-a} \otimes V_{b-a} = \mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a}) \oplus \Lambda^2(V_{b-a}), $$
    where $\Lambda^2(V_{b-a})$ denotes the exterior square of $\Lambda^2(V_{b-a})$. By definition, $\iota_{V_{b-a}}$ acts by $+1$ on $\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a})$ and by $-1$ on $\Lambda^2(V_{b-a})$.
    Following \cite{FultonHarris}, 11.1, we show that for all integer $n$
    $$\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{n}) = \bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} V_{2n-4i}.$$
    The weights of $V_{n}$ are $n, n-2, \dots, -n+2, -n$, hence the weights of $V_n \otimes V_n$ are of the form 
    $$\alpha +\beta , \ \text{with} \ \alpha, \beta \in \{n, n-2, \dots, -n+2, -n\},$$
    we can arrange them in a matrix as follows
    $$E := \begin{pmatrix}
        2n & 2n-2 & 2n-4 & \cdots & 0 \\
        2n-2 & 2n-4 & 2n-6 & \cdots & -2 \\
        2n-4 & 2n-6 & 2n-8 &  \cdots & -4 \\
        \vdots & \vdots &  & \ddots &  \vdots \\
        0 & -2 & -4 & \cdots & -2n
    \end{pmatrix}$$
    and remark that the weights of $\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a})$ are given by the upper triangular matrix
    $$\begin{pmatrix}
        2n & 2n-2 & 2n-4 & \cdots & 0 \\
        * & 2n-4 & 2n-6 & \cdots & -2 \\
        * & * & 2n-8 &  \cdots & -4 \\
        \vdots & \vdots &  & \ddots &  \vdots \\
        * & * & * & \cdots & -2n
    \end{pmatrix}.$$
    As the representations are entirely determined by their eigenvalues, we can identify the irreducible components of $\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a})$. Namely, the first line of $E$ together with the last column give 
    $$2n, 2n-2, \dots, -2n$$
    as eigenvalues, corresponding to $V_{2n}$. We then take the second line and the $(n-1)$-th column and obtain $V_{2n-4}$. We iterate this step until the $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$-th line and column. This shows the formula 
    $$\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{n}) \cong \bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} V_{2n-4i}.$$
    We deduce from that that for all $i \in \{0, \dots, b-a\}$,
    $$\iota_{V_{b-a}}\vert_{V_{2i}} = (-1)^{b-a+i}\mathrm{Id}_{V_{2i}}.$$
    
    \end{proof}

    Finally, we have 
    $$V_{\Tilde{\psi}}\otimes V_{\Tilde{\psi}}\otimes V_{b-a}\otimes V_{b-a} \cong \bigoplus_{m=0}^{b-a}(V_{\Tilde{\psi}}\otimes V_{\Tilde{\psi}})\otimes V_{2b-2a-2m}$$
    and 
    $$\mathrm{As}^-(\Tilde{\psi}_I) \cong \bigoplus_{m=0}^{b-a}\mathrm{As}^{(-1)^{m+1}}(\Tilde{\psi} \vert \cdot\vert^{\frac{a+b}{2}})\otimes \mathrm{Sym}^{2b-2a-2m}.$$
    In terms of segments, it becomes
    $$\mathrm{As}^-(\Tilde{\psi}_I) \cong \bigoplus_{m=0}^{b-a}\mathrm{As}^{(-1)^{m+1}}(\Tilde{\psi})\otimes [2a+m, 2b-m].$$
    Hence, 
    $$L(s, \Tilde{\psi}\otimes I, \mathrm{As}^-) = \prod_{m=0}^{b-a} L(s+2b-m, \Tilde{\psi},\mathrm{As}^{(-1)^{m+1}}).$$

    $$V_{b-a} \otimes V_{b-a} = \mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a}) \oplus \Lambda^2(V_{b-a}), $$
    where $\Lambda^2(V_{b-a})$ denotes the exterior square of $\Lambda^2(V_{b-a})$. By definition, $\iota_{V_{b-a}}$ acts by $+1$ on $\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a})$ and by $-1$ on $\Lambda^2(V_{b-a})$.
    Following \cite{FultonHarris}, 11.1, we show that for all integer $n$
    $$\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{n}) = \bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} V_{2n-4i}.$$
    The weights of $V_{n}$ are $n, n-2, \dots, -n+2, -n$, hence the weights of $V_n \otimes V_n$ are of the form 
    $$\alpha +\beta , \ \text{with} \ \alpha, \beta \in \{n, n-2, \dots, -n+2, -n\},$$
    we can arrange them in a matrix as follows
    $$E := \begin{pmatrix}
        2n & 2n-2 & 2n-4 & \cdots & 0 \\
        2n-2 & 2n-4 & 2n-6 & \cdots & -2 \\
        2n-4 & 2n-6 & 2n-8 &  \cdots & -4 \\
        \vdots & \vdots &  & \ddots &  \vdots \\
        0 & -2 & -4 & \cdots & -2n
    \end{pmatrix}$$
    and remark that the weights of $\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a})$ are given by the upper triangular matrix
    $$\begin{pmatrix}
        2n & 2n-2 & 2n-4 & \cdots & 0 \\
        * & 2n-4 & 2n-6 & \cdots & -2 \\
        * & * & 2n-8 &  \cdots & -4 \\
        \vdots & \vdots &  & \ddots &  \vdots \\
        * & * & * & \cdots & -2n
    \end{pmatrix}.$$
    As the representations are entirely determined by their eigenvalues, we can identify the irreducible components of $\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{b-a})$. Namely, the first line of $E$ together with the last column give 
    $$2n, 2n-2, \dots, -2n$$
    as eigenvalues, corresponding to $V_{2n}$. We then take the second line and the $(n-1)$-th column and obtain $V_{2n-4}$. We iterate this step until the $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$-th line and column. This shows the formula 
    $$\mathrm{Sym}^2(V_{n}) \cong \bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} V_{2n-4i}.$$
    We deduce from that that for all $i \in \{0, \dots, b-a\}$,
    $$\iota_{V_{b-a}}\vert_{V_{2i}} = (-1)^{b-a+i}\mathrm{Id}_{V_{2i}}.$$

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $E \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a finite multiset. Then, there exists a unique partition of $E$ into segments, 
        $$E = I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d,$$
        such that none of the segments $I_i$ are linked.
head: environment
name: Decomposition in maximal segments

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x=\max(E)$, and take $y$ such that $[y, x] \subset E $ is maximal for this property. Set $E'=E ackslash [y, x]$, by induction $E'$ admits a unique partition $E'=I'_1\cup \cdots \cup I'_d$ such that none of the segments are linked. As $E=E'\cup [y, x]$, we have to show that for all $i\in \{1, \dots, d\}$, $I'_i$ is not linked to $[y, x]$. Suppose that there exists $i\in \{1, \dots, d\}$, such that $I'_i$ is linked to $[y, x]$, therefore there exists $z\in I'_i$, such that $z<y$ and $[z, x]\subset E$. But then $[z, x]$ is longer than $[y, x]$, which is not possible by assumption on $y$. Hence, the partition $E=I'_1\cup \cdots \cup I'_d\cup [y, x]$ works. To show the uniqueness of this decomposition, suppose that $E=I_1\cup \cdots\cup I_d$ is such that none of the $I_i$'s are linked and for all $i\in\{1, \dots, d\}$, $I_i 
ot = [y, x]$. Hence, there exist $i
ot = j$ such that $y\in I_i$ and $x\in I_j$. As $E$ contains all the integers between $y$ and $x$, there exists $n\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $y+n \in I_i$ and $y+n+1
ot \in I_i$ that is $y+n+1\in I_k$ with $k
ot = i$. Then the segments $I_i$ and $I_k$ are linked, which contradicts the assumption on the $I_i$'s.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Tilde{\psi}\in \mathrm{Irr}_u(W_E)$ be conjugate-dual, that is $\Tilde{\psi}\cong \Tilde{\psi}^*$ and therefore $E=-E$. We prove the existence and unicity of such a partition of $E$ by induction. Let $x=\max(E)$, and take $y\in E$ such that $[ y, x ] \subset E$ and $[ y,x ] $ is of maximal length. Then, there are two possibilities, either $y\not = -x$ or $y =-x$.
        \begin{itemize}
            \item  If $y\not = -x$, then by symmetry $[-x, -y]\subset E$ and the segments $[-x, -y]$ and $[ y, x ]$ are not linked. Indeed, if they were linked, then $[ -x, -y ] \cup [ y, x ] =[ -x, -x ] \subset E$, which is impossible by hypothesis. Set $E' = E\backslash ([ -x, -y ]\cup [ y, x ])$, we have $E'=-E'$. Suppose by induction that $E'$ admits a unique decomposition $E'=I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d$ satisfying all the properties of the lemma, and denote by $S'$ this partition. Then $S = S'\cup \{[ -x, -y ], [ y, x ]\} $ is a partition of $E$, it follows directly that the first property is preserved for $S$. The second property is given by the fact that all the symmetric segments of the partition $S$ are in $S'$. It remains to show that $[ y, x ]$ is not linked to a $I_i$, for any $i\in\{1, \dots, d\}$ (it will imply also that $[ -x,-y]$ is not linked to any other segment in the decomposition). Assume that there exists $i\in \{1, \dots d\}$ such that $I_i$ is linked to $[ y,x]$, then $y-1\in I_i$ because $x=\max(E)$. But then $[ y-1, x] \subset E$ and its length is superior to the length of $[ y, x]$, which is not possible. Hence property 3 is also satisfied, because the only linked segments involved in the decomposition of $E$ are the ones inherited from $E'$. 
            
            Let us now prove the unicity. Suppose we have a partition $S_{\tilde{\psi}}$ of $E$ satisfying conditions 1, 2 and 3. To prove the unicity of $S_{\tilde{\psi}}$, it suffices to show, by induction again, that $ [x,y] \in S_{\tilde{\psi}}$. Let $I\in S_{\tilde{\psi}}$ containing $x$ and of maximal length. We have $\max I= x$ by assumption, and we can assume that $y = \min I-1$. As $[y,x] \subset E$, there exists $J\in S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$, such that $y\in J$, meaning that $I$ and $J$ are linked. By property 3, $J=-I$ so $-x \in J$ and the union of $I$ and $J$ is $[ -x, x ]$, which is not possible by assumption on $y$. That proves that $I=[ y,x]$, therefore the decomposition is unique.

            \item Assume now that $y=-x$, and $\Tilde{\psi}$ is conjugate-symplectic, i.e. $\mathrm{sgn}(\tilde{\psi})=-1$ which implies that $0$ has even multiplicity in $E$. We denote $m>0$ the largest integer such that $E$ contains all the elements of $[ -x, x ]$ with multiplicity at least $m$, and define $m[ -x,x] = [ -x,x] \sqcup \cdots \sqcup [ -x,x] $. 
            
            We have $\mathrm{sgn}[ -x,x]=1$, unless $x\in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}\backslash \mathbb{Z}$. Suppose $x\in \mathbb{Z}$, then $0\in[ -x,x]$. If the multiplicity $m$ of $[ -x,x]$ is odd, then there exists $z < x$ such that 
            $$[ -z,z]\subset E\backslash(m[ -x,x]),$$
            because $0$ has even multiplicity in $E$, and we take $z$ maximal for this property. Now set 
            $$E'=E\backslash ((m-1)[ -x,x]\sqcup[ -x,z]\sqcup [ -z,x]).$$
            We have $E'=-E'$ and the multiplicity of $0$ is still even. Suppose by induction, that $E'$ admits a unique decomposition $E'=I_1\sqcup \cdots \sqcup I_d$ satisfying all the properties of the lemma. Then the partition of $E$
            $$S_{\Tilde{\psi}}=\{I_1, \dots, I_d,(m-1)[ -x,x],[ -x,z],[ -z,x]\}$$
            automatically verifies properties 1 and 2. Note that if there exists $i\in \{1, \dots, d\}$ such that $I_i$ is linked to $[ -z, x]$ then either there exists an element $t\in I_i$ such that $t>x$ which is impossible, or there exists $t\in I_i$ such that $t<-z$ but in that case $-t>z$ which means that the segment $[ -t, t] \subset E\backslash(m[-x,x])$ is longer than $[ -z, z]$ and it is also impossible. If there exists $k\in \{1, \dots, d\}$ such that $I_k=[ -z,x]$ then $-I_k=[ -x,z]$ also appears but then $(m+1)[ -x,x]\subset E$ which is not possible by definition of $m$. This implies in particular that the third condition is still verified. Hence, the partition $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ satisfies all the conditions. 
            
            If $\mathrm{sgn}([ -x,x])=-1$, i.e. $x\in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}\backslash \mathbb{Z}$, then $0\not \in [ -x,x]$. We set 
            $$E'= E\backslash[ -x, x ]$$
            and decompose it as 
            $$E'=I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d$$
            satisfying all properties by induction. As $[-x,x]$ contains all the $I_i$ by assumption, it follows directly that $E = I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d \cup [-x,x]$ is a partition satisfying our conditions. 

            It remains to show that the partition $S_{\tilde{\psi}}$ given by the above algorithm is the unique one satisfying conditions 1, 2 and 3. Suppose that $E = I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d$ is another decomposition such that properties 1, 2 and 3 are satisfied. Let $I_i = [ y, x]$ be a segment containing $x$. We show that $I_i\in S_{\tilde{\psi}}$, i.e. that either  $y=-x$ and the multiplicity $m_i$ of $I_i$ is even, or $y=-z$, where $[-z,z]$ is maximal in $E\backslash (m[-x,x])$, with $m_i=1$. Recall that here, we have $[-x,x]\subset E$. In that case, either $I_i =-I_i$, or $I_i$ and $-I_i$ are linked because there exists a segment $I_k$ containing $y-1$, hence linked to $I_i$ and property 3 says that $I_k=-I_i$. Thanks to the second property, if $I_i=-I_i$, i.e. $y=-x$, then $m_i$ is even. If $I_i$ is linked to $-I_i$ then by the definition of $z$ there exists a segment $I_k$ containing $z$, and $-z\leq y \leq z<x$, forcing $I_k$ to be linked with $I_i$. Using the third property we have $I_k=-I_i$, hence $-z=y$, and $m_i=1$. Therefore, $I_i\in S_{\tilde{\psi}}$, the partition $S_{\Tilde{\psi}}$ is unique.

            \item Assume that $y=-x$, and $\tilde{\psi}$ is conjugate-orthogonal, i.e. $\mathrm{sgn}(\tilde{\psi})=1$. 
            
            If $\mathrm{sgn}[-x,x]=-1$, then $x\in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}\backslash\mathbb{Z}$. Suppose $[-x,x]$ appears with odd multiplicity $m$. If there exists $z \in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}\backslash \mathbb{Z}, \  z<x$ such that 
            $$[ -z, z] \subset E\backslash m[-x, x],$$ 
            we take $z$ maximal for this property. Then we set 
            $$E' = E\backslash ((m-1)[ -x,x] \cup [ -x,z]\cup [ -z,x])$$
            and suppose by induction that $E'$ admits a partition satisfying properties 1, 2 and 3, $E' = I_1 \cup\cdots \cup I_d $. We have 
            $$E= I_1 \cup\cdots \cup I_d \cup (m-1)[ -x,x] \cup [ -x,z]\cup [ -z,x]$$
            satisfying automatically properties 1 and 2. If there exists $i\in \{1, \dots, d\}$ such that $I_i$ is linked to $[ -z, x]$ then either there exists an element $t\in I_i$ such that $t>x$ which is impossible, or there exists $t\in I_i$ such that $t<-z$ but in that case $-t>z$ which means that the segment $[ -t, t] \subset E$ is longer than $[ -z, z]$ and it is also impossible. If, there exists $k\in \{1, \dots, d\}$ such that $I_k=[ -z,x]$ then $-I_k=[ -x,z]$ also appears but then $(m+1)[ -x,x]\subset E$ which is not possible by definition of $m$. This implies in particular that the third condition is still verified. Hence, the partition $$S_{\Tilde{\psi}}=\{I_1,\dots, I_d, (m-1)[ -x,x],[ -x,z], [ -z,x]\}$$
            satisfies all the conditions. If such an element $z$ does not exists in $E$, then we set 
            $$E'=E\backslash ((m-1)[ -x,x]\cup[ -x,-\frac{1}{2}]\cup [ \frac{1}{2},x]).$$ 
            The induction works in the same way.

             If $[ -x,x]$ is of odd length, then we set $E'= E\backslash[ -x, x ]$ and decompose it as $E'=I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d$ satisfying properties 1, 2, and 3, by induction. As $[-x,x]$ contains all the $I_i$ by assumption, it follows directly that $E = I_1\cup \cdots \cup I_d \cup [-x,x]$ is a partition satisfying our conditions. 

             The proof of the unicity of the partition is the same as in the case of $\Tilde{\psi}$ conjugate-symplectic.

        \end{itemize}

label: closedim
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{closedim}
    The map $CBC: \Omega_{\mathrm{gen}}(U(n)) \to  \Omega(G_n(E))$ is a closed immersion.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First of all, note that by the previous proposition, $CBC$ is injective, hence the images of two different connected components in $\Omega_{\mathrm{gen}}(U(n))$ don't intersect. Therefore, it suffices to show that the map from a connected component $\Omega\subset \Omega_{\mathrm{gen}}(U(n))$ to the corresponding component $\Omega' \subset \Omega(G_n(E))$ is a closed immersion.
    Let $[M, \sigma]$ be an element of $\Omega_{\mathrm{gen}}(U(n))$, with

    $$M=G_{n_1}\times \cdots \times G_{n_k} \times U(m),$$
    and we decompose 

    $$\sigma = \sigma_1 \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \sigma_k \boxtimes \sigma_u.$$
    We choose a pair $(L,\rho)$ as a representative of $\mathbf{Cs}(BC(\sigma_u))$, with $L$ a Levi subgroup of $G_m$, and $\rho$ an irreducible and supercuspidal representation of $L$, such that
    $$\mathcal{M}=G_{n_1}^2\times \cdots \times G_{n_k}^2 \times L, \ \mathrm{and} \ \tau = \sigma_1 \boxtimes \sigma_1^* \cdots \boxtimes \sigma_k \boxtimes \sigma_k^* \boxtimes \rho,$$
    is a representative of the image of $[M, \sigma]$ through $CBC$. If we set
    $$W(M, \sigma)=\{w \in W_G(M) : \ \exists \chi \in \mathcal{X}(M), \ \sigma^w = \sigma \otimes \chi \}$$
    the connected component $\Omega_\sigma$ can then be described as a quotient of a complex torus by a finite group
    $$\Omega_\sigma = \mathcal{X}(M)\otimes \sigma/W(M, \sigma).$$
    By adapting those definition to $G_n(E)$, we also get 
    $$\Omega_\tau =  \mathcal{X}(\mathcal{M})\otimes \tau/W(\mathcal{M}, \tau).$$
    Consider the following commuting diagram 

    $$\xymatrix{   \Omega_\sigma \ar[r]  & \Omega_\tau \\
    \mathcal{X}(M)\otimes \sigma \ar[u] \ar[r] & \mathcal{X}(\mathcal{M})\otimes \tau \ar[u]
    }$$
    where $\mathcal{X}(M)\otimes \sigma$ (resp. $\mathcal{X}(\mathcal{M})\otimes \tau$) is the orbit of $\sigma$ (resp. $\tau$) under the action of $\mathcal{X}(M)$ (resp. $\mathcal{X}(\mathcal{M})$), and the left and right maps are the canonical projections. The evaluation at a uniformizer of $E$ allows us to identify $\mathcal{X}(M)$ with $(\mathbb{C}^\times)^{k}$ and $\mathcal{X(M)}$ with $(\mathbb{C}^\times)^{2k+r}$. Therefore, the base-change map gives rise to the bottom map of the diagram above, defined by

    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
         & \mathcal{X}(M) \otimes \sigma & \longrightarrow & \mathcal{X}(\mathcal{M})\otimes \tau  \\
         & (\chi_1, \dots, \chi_k)\otimes \sigma & \longmapsto & (\chi_1, \chi_1^{-1} \dots, \chi_k,\chi_k^{-1}, 1, \dots ,1)\otimes \tau
    \end{array}$$
    
    Let us describe the corresponding map between $\Omega_\sigma$ and $\Omega_\tau$. Denote by $\Sigma$ the set of isomorphism classes of the $\sigma_i$'s and for all $\nu \in \Sigma$

    $$m_\sigma(\nu):= \vert \{1\leq i \leq k, \nu \cong \sigma_i \}\vert.$$
    Up to twisting $\sigma$ by an unramified character, we can assume that for all $i\in\{1, \dots, k\}$ either $\sigma_i\cong \sigma_i^*$, or $\sigma_i^* \not \in \mathcal{X}(G_{n_i})\otimes \sigma_i$, and that for all $i,j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$ either $\sigma_i \cong \sigma_j$ or $\sigma_i, \sigma_i^*\not \in \mathcal{X}(G_{n_j})\otimes \sigma_j$. Then we have 

    $$\Omega_\sigma \cong \prod_{\underset{\nu \cong \nu^*}{\nu \in \Sigma}} (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\sigma(\nu)}/ (S_{m_\sigma(\nu)}\ltimes (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{m_\sigma(\nu)}) \times \prod_{\underset{\nu \not\cong \nu^*}{\nu \in \Sigma}} (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\sigma(\nu)}/ S_{m_\sigma(\nu)},$$
    where for all integers $l$, $S_{l}$ is the permutation group that acts on $(\mathbb{C^\times})^l$ by 
    $$s \cdot (x_1, \dots, x_l) = (x_{s(1)}, \dots, x_{s(l)}),$$
    and the action of $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{l}$ on $(\mathbb{C^\times})^l$ is given by the action of $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ on $\mathbb{C}^\times$, namely
    $$\overline{1}\cdot x = x^{-1}, \ x\in \mathbb{C}^\times$$
    $\overline{1}$ being the non-trivial element in $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
    
    We can do the same in $G_n(E)$. If $\tau= \tau_1 \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \tau_{k'}$, with $k'=2k+r$, and $\Sigma'$ the set of isomorphism classes of the $\tau_i$'s. Again, up to twisting $\tau$ by an unramified character, we can assume that for all $i,j\in\{1, \dots, k'\}$ either $\tau_i\cong \tau_j$, or $\tau_i \not \in \mathcal{X}(G_{n_j})\otimes \sigma_j$. We get 

    $$\Omega_\tau \cong \prod_{\nu' \in \Sigma'} (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\tau(\nu')}/ S_{m_\tau(\nu')}.$$
    In our case, we have $\tau = CBC(\sigma)$, hence $\Sigma \subseteq \Sigma'$, and we want to show that the corresponding map 
    $$\prod_{\underset{\nu \cong \nu^*}{\nu \in \Sigma}} (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\sigma(\nu)}/ (S_{m_\sigma(\nu)}\ltimes (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{m_\sigma(\nu)}) \times \prod_{\underset{\nu \not\cong \nu^*}{\nu \in \Sigma}} (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\sigma(\nu)}/ S_{m_\sigma(\nu)} \to  \prod_{\nu' \in \Sigma'} (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\tau(\nu')}/ S_{m_\tau(\nu')}$$
    is a closed immersion. On one hand, a block of the form 
    
    $$(\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\sigma(\nu)}/ S_{m_\sigma(\nu)}$$
    is sent to a block of the form 
    
    $$(\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\sigma(\nu)}/ S_{m_\sigma(\nu)} \times (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\sigma(\nu)}/ S_{m_\sigma(\nu)},$$
    through the closed immersion $(x_1, \dots,x_{m_\sigma(\nu)}) \mapsto (x_1, \dots,x_{m_\sigma(\nu)},x_1^{-1}, \dots,x_{m_\sigma(\nu)}^{-1})$.
    On the other hand, a block of the form 
    
    $$(\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\sigma(\nu)}/ (S_{m_\sigma(\nu)}\ltimes (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{m_\sigma(\nu)})$$
    is sent to a block of the form 
    $$(\mathbb{C}^\times)^{2m_\sigma(\nu)+\alpha_\nu}/ S_{2m_\sigma(\nu)+\alpha_\nu}$$
    through the map $(x_1, \dots,x_{m_\sigma(\nu)}) \mapsto (x_1,x_1^{-1} \dots,x_{m_\sigma(\nu)}, x_{m_\sigma(\nu)}^{-1}, 1, \dots, 1)$. We can decompose this map as 
    
    $$
     (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{m_\sigma(\nu)}/ (S_{m_\sigma(\nu)}\ltimes (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{m_\sigma(\nu)}) \to  (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{2m_\sigma(\nu)}/ S_{2m_\sigma(\nu)} \to  (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{2m_\sigma(\nu)+\alpha_\nu}/ S_{2m_\sigma(\nu)+\alpha_\nu}
     $$

     $$
     (x_1, \dots,x_{m_\sigma(\nu)}) \mapsto (x_1,x_1^{-1}, \dots,x_{m_\sigma(\nu)}, x_{m_\sigma(\nu)}^{-1}) \mapsto (x_1,x_1^{-1}, \dots,x_{m_\sigma(\nu)}, x_{m_\sigma(\nu)}^{-1}, 1, \dots, 1)
     $$
     

                                                                                                                                                                                        
    Let us denote $m=m_\sigma(\nu)$, it remains to show that the map
    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
         & (\mathbb{C}^\times)^m/(S_m\ltimes (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^m) & \longrightarrow & (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{2m}/S_{2m}  \\
         & (x_1, \dots,x_{m}) & \longmapsto & (x_1,x_1^{-1} \dots,x_{m}, x_{m}^{-1})
    \end{array}$$
    is a closed immersion. We identify $(\mathbb{C}^\times)^m/(S_m\ltimes (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^m)$ with the set of unitary polynomials of degree $m$, namely
    $$\left\{Q(T) = \prod_{i=1}^m(T-(x_i+x_i^{-1})), \ x_i\in \mathbb{C}^\times\right\}.$$
    Similarly, we identify $(\mathbb{C}^\times)^{2m}/S_{2m}$ with unitary polynomials $P$ of degree $2m$ and such that $P(0) \not = 0$. The image of the map $(x_1, \dots,x_{m}) \mapsto (x_1,x_1^{-1} \dots,x_{m}, x_{m}^{-1})$ through this identification is given by
    $$\left\{P(T) = \prod_{i=1}^m(T-x_i)(T-x_i^{-1}), \ x_i\in \mathbb{C}^\times\right\}.$$
    Remark that 
    $$P(T)= T^{2m}P(T^{-1}),$$
    ensures that this image is indeed closed. Through these identifications, the map is given by
    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
         
         & Q & \longmapsto &  T^mQ(T+T^{-1}) = P(T) 
    \end{array}$$
    It is indeed a closed immersion because the inverse map is given by
    $$P \mapsto R(T) = T^{-m}P(T), $$
    and we have 
    $$R(T^{-1})=R(T).$$
    Hence $R$ is invariant under the inversion $T \mapsto T^{-1}$, in other words
    $$R \in \mathbb{C}[T, T^{-1}]^{\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}} \cong \mathbb{C}[T+T^{-1}]\cong \mathbb{C}[T].$$

title: Definition
body_md: Let $X$ be a reduced commutative noetherian $\mathbb{C}$-algebra. A $(G,X)$-module is a $\mathbb{C}$-vector space $\mathcal{V}$ with a smooth representation $(\pi, \mathcal{V})$ of $G$ together with a structure of flat $X$-module where both actions commute.
head: environment
name: $(G, X)$-modules

title: Definition
body_md: A function $F : \mathcal{X}(M) \to i_Q^G(\rho \otimes \chi)$ is regular if its image in $V$ is finite-dimensional and if it is regular in each variable.
head: environment

label: SectionReg
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{SectionReg}
The following statements are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The function
$$
\begin{array}{cccc}
F : & \mathcal{X}(M) & \to & i_Q^G(\rho \otimes \chi) \\
& \chi & \mapsto & v_\chi
\end{array}
$$
is regular.

\item There exists a compact open subgroup $K \subset G$ such that $v_\chi$ is $K$-invariant for all $\chi \in \mathcal{X}(M)$, and for all $g \in G$ and all $e^\vee \in \rho^\vee$,

$$
\chi \mapsto \langle v_\chi(g), e^\vee \rangle
$$
is regular.

\item There exists $v \in i_Q^G(\rho_X)$ such that for all $\chi \in \mathcal{X}(M)$, $v_\chi = \mathrm{sp}_\chi(v)$, where $\mathrm{sp}_\chi$ denotes the canonical morphism from $i_Q^G(\rho_X)$ to $i_Q^G(\rho \otimes \chi)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us show that (1) implies (2). By definition of the induced representation, for every character $\chi \in \mathcal{X}(M)$ there exists a compact open subgroup $K_\chi \subset G$ such that $v_\chi$ is $K_\chi$-invariant. Since $K_0$ is maximal, we have $K_\chi \subset K_0$. By assumption, $\mathrm{Im}(F) \subset V$ is of dimension $d$, so we fix a basis $\{v_1, \dots, v_d\}$ and denote by $K_i$ a compact subgroup fixing $v_i$. Let $K'=\cap_{i=1}^d K_i$. Thus, $v_\chi$ is $K'$-invariant for all $\chi \in \mathcal{X}(M)$. Moreover, since $F$ is regular in each variable, the condition
$$
\chi \mapsto \langle v_\chi(g), e^\vee \rangle, \quad g \in G, \ e^\vee \in \rho^\vee
$$
is simply a reformulation.

Let us show that (2) implies (1). Let $K'$ be a compact open subgroup of $G$ such that $v_\chi$ is $K'$-invariant for all $\chi \in \mathcal{X}(M)$. Then for all $\chi \in \mathcal{X}(M)$,
$$
v_\chi \in i_Q^G(\rho \otimes \chi)^{K'} \cong V^{K'}.
$$
Hence, the image of $F$ is finite-dimensional. For all $g \in G$ and all $e^\vee \in \rho^\vee$, define
$$
\begin{array}{cccc}
\langle \mathbf{ev}_g(\cdot), e^\vee \rangle : & V & \longrightarrow & \mathbb{C} \\
& v_\chi & \longmapsto & \langle v_\chi(g), e^\vee \rangle
\end{array}
$$
By assumption, the composition
$$
\langle \mathbf{ev}_g(\cdot), e^\vee \rangle \circ F : \chi \mapsto \langle v_\chi(g), e^\vee \rangle
$$
is regular for all $g \in G$ and all $e^\vee \in \rho^\vee$. Since the family
$$
\{\langle \mathbf{ev}_g(\cdot), e^\vee \rangle, \ g \in G, \ e^\vee \in \rho^\vee\}
$$
generates $V^*$, the function $F$ is regular.

To prove the equivalence between (3) and (1), it suffices to show that (1) implies (3). Let $\chi \in \mathcal{X}(M)$ and denote by $\phi_\chi$ the isomorphism between $i_Q^G(\rho \otimes \chi)$ and $i^{K_0}_{K_0\cap Q}(\rho)$. Let $\{v_1, \dots, v_d\}$ be a basis of the image of $F$ in $V = i^{K_0}_{K_0\cap Q}(\rho)$, and $\{v_{\chi,1}, \dots, v_{\chi,d}\}$ the corresponding basis in $i_Q^G(\rho \otimes \chi)$. We know that
$$
\phi_\chi(v_\chi)= \sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_{i,\chi} v_i,
$$
with $\lambda_i : \chi \mapsto \lambda_{i,\chi}$ regular since $F$ is regular, by assumption. Set $v_{X,i} = v_i \otimes \lambda_i$. We have an isomorphism of $(G,X)$-modules
$$
\phi_X : i_Q^G(\rho_X) \to i_{K_0\cap Q}^{K_0}(\rho) \otimes X.
$$
For each $i \in \{1, \dots, d\}$, define
$$
w_i = \phi_X^{-1}(v_i \otimes \lambda_i).
$$
Then we obtain
$$
\mathrm{sp}_\chi(v_i) = \phi_\chi^{-1}(v_i) \otimes \lambda_{i,\chi} = \lambda_{i,\chi} v_{\chi,i}.
$$
This completes the proof of the lemma.

label: Whittreg
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Whittreg}
    Let $Q=MU$ be a standard parabolic subgroup of $G$ and $\sigma\in\mathrm{Irr}_{\mathrm{gen}}(M)$. Denote $\pi_\chi=i_Q^G(\sigma\otimes \chi)$. There exists a regular section $\chi\in \mathcal{X}(M)\mapsto v_\chi \in \pi_\chi$, such that $\Tilde{J}_{\sigma_\chi}^{\psi_n}(v_\chi) = W_{f, \pi_\chi}^1$, for some $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We identify $\pi_\chi^\vee$ with $i_Q^G(\sigma^\vee\otimes \chi^{-1})$ via the pairing
    $$\langle v, v^\vee\rangle_{\pi_\chi} = \int_{Q\backslash G}\langle v(g), v^\vee(g) \rangle dg.$$
    If we denote $\mathcal{B}(\pi_\chi)$ a basis of $\pi_\chi^{K}$ (we will denote $v^\vee$ the corresponding elements in the dual basis of $\mathcal{B}(\pi_\chi)$), where $K$ is a compact-open subgroup of $G$ for which  $f$ is right-invariant, then we have 
    $$W_{f,\pi_\chi}^1(g)=\sum_{v \in \mathcal{B}(\pi_\chi)} \int^*_N \langle \pi_\chi(ug)\pi_\chi(f^\vee)v, v^\vee \rangle_{\pi_\chi}\psi_n(u)^{-1}du.$$
    By Proposition 2.8 in \cite{LapidMao}, 
    $$W_{f,\pi_\chi}^1(g)=\sum_{v \in \mathcal{B}(\pi_\chi)}J_{\sigma \otimes \chi}^{\psi_n}(\pi_\chi(g)\pi_\chi(f^\vee)v). J_{\sigma^\vee\otimes\chi^{-1}}^{\psi_n^{-1}}(v^\vee)$$
    but
    $$J_{\sigma_\chi}^{\psi_n}(\pi_\chi(g)\pi_\chi(f^\vee)v) = \Tilde{J}_{\sigma_\chi}^{\psi_n} (\pi_\chi(f^\vee)v)(g),$$
    therefore
    $$W_{f,\pi_\chi}^1(g)=\Tilde{J}_{\sigma_\chi}^{\psi_n}\left(\sum_{v \in \mathcal{B}(\pi_\chi)} J_{\sigma^\vee\otimes\chi^{-1}}^{\psi_n^{-1}}(v^\vee).\pi_\chi(f^\vee)v\right).$$

label: GKfam
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{GKfam}
    Let A be a complex algebra of finite type, and denote by
    $$C^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n, A, \psi_n)$$
    the $(P_n, A)$-module of smooth functions $f:P_n\to A$ such that 
    $$f(up)= \psi_n(u)f(p), \ p\in P_n, \ u\in N_n$$
    on which $P_n$ acts by right translation and $A$ by pointwise multiplication, and both actions commute. If $V\subseteq C^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n, A, \psi_n)$ is a sub-$(P_n, A)$-module, such that for all $p\in P_n$, 
    $$ev_p(V)=\{f(p), \ f\in V\} = A,$$ 
    then $V$ contains $C_c^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n, A, \psi_n)$.
head: environment
name: Family version of Gelfand-Kazhdan

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $n\in \mathbb{N}^*$, and suppose that that the theorem is true for all $k<n$. Let $U_n$ be the unipotent radical of $P_n$ of matrices of the form 
    $$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \cdots & 0 & * \\
                  \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
                  0 & \cdots & 1 & * \\
                  0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$
    such that $P_n = G_{n-1}U_n$ and $U_n\cong F^{n-1}$. We have a surjective map
    $$N_n\backslash P_n = N_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1} \longrightarrow P_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1}.$$
    The action of $G_{n-1}$ on $F^{n-1}$ admits two orbits : $\{0\}$ and $F^{n-1}\backslash \{0\}$. The mirabolic subgroup can be seen as a stabilizer under this action, 
    $$P_{n-1}=\mathrm{Stab}_{G_{n-1}}\left( (0, \dots, 0, 1) \right), $$
    then we have an isomorphism
    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
         & P_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1} & \longrightarrow & F^{n-1}\backslash \{0\} \\
         & P_{n-1}g & \longmapsto & (0, \dots, 0, 1)g
    \end{array}$$
    Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(U_n, A)=C_c^\infty(F^{n-1}, A)$, $f\in V$ (note that $R(\varphi)f\in V$), and $g\in G_{n-1}$. We compute 
    \begin{align*}
        (R(\varphi)f)\begin{pmatrix}
            g & 0 \\ 0 & 1
        \end{pmatrix} & = \int_{F^{n-1}} \varphi(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})f\left(\begin{pmatrix}
            g & \\ & 1
        \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
            1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & x_1 \\
             & \ddots & \ddots &\vdots & \vdots \\
             & & \ddots &0 & x_{n-1} \\
             & & & & 1
        \end{pmatrix}\right)d(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}), \\
        & = \int_{F^{n-1}} \varphi(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) \psi\left(e_{n-1}g.\begin{pmatrix}
            x_1 \\ \vdots \\ x_{n-1}
        \end{pmatrix}\right)d(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) f\left(\begin{pmatrix}
            g & \\ & 1
        \end{pmatrix}\right), \\
        & = \hat{\varphi}(e_{n-1}g)f\left(\begin{pmatrix}
            g & \\ & 1
        \end{pmatrix}\right),
    \end{align*}
    where $\hat{\varphi}$ is the Fourier transform of $\varphi$ with respect to $\psi$. Recall that the Fourier transform 
    $$\varphi \mapsto \hat{\varphi}$$
    is an isomorphism of $C_c^\infty(F^{n-1}, A)$ to itself. By the identification $P_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1}\cong F^{n-1}\backslash \{0\}$, we get 
    $$C_c^\infty(P_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1}, A) \subset C_c^\infty(F^{n-1}, A).$$
    Therefore, this shows that the representation $V$ is fixed under multiplication by elements of $C_c^\infty(P_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1}, A)$. 

    Now, suppose that $f\in C_c^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n,A, \psi_n)\cong C_c^\infty(N_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1}, A, \psi_{n-1})$. The image of the support of $f$ is compact in $N_{n-1} \backslash G_{n-1}$, hence, considering the projection $$\mathbf{p}: N_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1} \to P_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1},$$ 
    its image is also compact in $P_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1}$. An element of $\mathbf{p}(\mathrm{Supp}(f))$ is of the form $P_{n-1}g$ with $g\in G_{n-1}$, and 
    $$\mathbf{p}^{-1}(P_{n-1}g)=N_{n-1}\backslash P_{n-1} g \cong N_{n-1}\backslash P_{n-1}.$$
    We consider the $(P_{n-1}, A)$-submodule of $C^\infty(N_{n-1}\backslash P_{n-1}, A, \psi_{n-1})$ 
    $$V_g=\{p\in P_{n-1}\mapsto h(pg), \ h \in V\}.$$
    For all $p\in P_{n-1}$, 
    $$ev_p(V_g)=ev_{pg}(V)=A.$$    
    By induction, this space $V_g$ contains $C_c^\infty(N_{n-1}\backslash P_{n-1}, A, \psi_{n-1})$. Finally, 
    $$f\vert_{P_{n-1}g}\in \{p\in P_{n-1}\mapsto h(pg), \ h \in V\}.$$
    In conclusion, we have shown that for all $g\in G_{n-1}$, there exists a function $h_g\in V$ such that 
    $$h_g\vert_{P_{n-1}g}=f\vert_{P_{n-1}g}.$$
    By smoothness of these functions, we deduce that for all $g\in G_{n-1}$, there exists $U_g$ is a neighborhood of $g$ in $P_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1}$, such that for all $g'\in U_g$
    $$h_g\vert_{P_{n-1}g'}=f\vert_{P_{n-1}g'}.$$
    As $\mathbf{p}(\mathrm{Supp}(f))$ is compact in $P_{n-1}\backslash G_{n-1}$, there exists $g_1, \dots, g_N\in \mathbf{p}(\mathrm{Supp}(f))$ such that 
    $$\mathbf{p}(\mathrm{Supp}(f))\subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^N U_{g_i}.$$
    We can also choose disjoint compact open neighborhoods $V_i\subseteq U_{g_i}$ such that 
    $$\mathbf{p}(\mathrm{Supp}(f))\subseteq \bigsqcup_{i=1}^N V_{i}.$$ 
    And finally, for all $i$, there exists $h_i=h_{g_i}\in V$ such that 
    $$h_i\vert_{\mathbf{p}^{-1}(V_i)}=f\vert_{\mathbf{p}^{-1}(V_i)}$$
    and 
    $$\mathrm{Supp}(f)\subseteq \bigsqcup_{i=1}^N\mathbf{p}^{-1}(V_i).$$
    Then $f=\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf{1}_{V_i}h_i \in V$, since $\mathbf{1}_{V_i}\in C_c^\infty(P_{n-1} \backslash G_{n-1}, A)$ and we have already seen that $V$ is invariant by multiplication by $C_c^\infty(P_{n-1} \backslash G_{n-1}, A)$.

label: CoroGKfamKirrilov
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{CoroGKfamKirrilov}
    Let $Q=LU$ be a parabolic subgroup of $G$, let $\rho\in \mathrm{Irr} (L)$ be generic, and let $X=\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{X}(L)]$. Then, the $(P_n, X)$-submodule $\mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho_X), \psi_n)\subset C^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n, X, \psi_n)$, contains $C_c^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n, X, \psi_n)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition, the application of the previous result is almost straightforward. It suffices to show that for all $p\in P_n$, the ideal $ev_p(\mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho_X), \psi_n))$ is equal to $X$. For all $\chi \in \mathcal{X}(L)$, denote by $m_\chi$ the corresponding maximal ideal in $X$, the specialization map 
    $$\mathrm{sp}_\chi : X \to X/m_\chi$$
    sends $\mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho_X), \psi_n)$ to $\mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \chi), \psi_n)$ which is non-zero because $\rho$ is generic. Therefore, $ev_p(\mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho_X), \psi_n))$ is not included in any of the maximal ideals of $X$, that is 
    $$ev_p(\mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho_X), \psi_n)) = X.$$
    Finally, by Proposition \ref{GKfam}, we obtain 
    $$C_c^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n, X, \psi_n)\subset\mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho_X), \psi_n)\subset C^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n, X, \psi_n).$$

label: CoroGKfam
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let 
    $$V:= \left\{W_{f, \pi_{X'}}^1 \vert_{P_n}, \ f \in C_c^\infty(G)\right\}\subset C^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n, X', \psi_n).$$
    To use the previous proposition, we show that $V$ is a $(P_n, X')$-module, such that for all $p\in P_n$, $ev_p(V)=X'$. Let $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, for all $p\in P_n$, we have 
    $$R(p)W_{f, \pi_{X'}}^1 = W_{R(p)f, \pi_{X'}}^1,$$
    and $C_c^\infty(G)$ is stable under right translation by $P_n$. Recall that the action of $\mathfrak{Z}(G)$ on $C_c^\infty(G)$, seen as a $G\times G$-representation, identifies $\mathfrak{Z}(G)$ with the algebra of endomorphisms of $C_c^\infty(G)$ (\cite{BDKV}, 1; \cite{Ren}, I.1.7). In other words, for all $z\in \mathfrak{Z}(G)$ (that can be seen as a regular function on $\Omega(G)$), we have 
    $$\pi_{X'}(z.f) = z(\mathbf{Cs}(\pi))\pi_{X'}(f), \ \ \mathrm{where} \ z(\mathbf{Cs}(\pi))\in \mathbb{C}.$$
    Therefore, 
    $$X' = X^{W(L, \rho)} = \mathbb{C}[\mathcal{X}(L)/W(L, \rho)]= \mathbb{C}[\Omega_\rho],$$
    acts on $V$ by 
    $$z. W_{f, \pi_{X'}}^1 = W_{z.f, \pi_{X'}}^1,$$
    and this action commutes with the action of $P_n$. It remains to show that for all $p\in P_n$, 
    $$ev_p(V) = \{W_{f, \pi_{X'}}^1(p), \ f \in C_c^\infty(G)\}=X'.$$
    Thanks to Lemma \ref{Whittreg}, for all parabolic subgroup $Q=LU$ of $G$ and all $\rho\in \mathrm{Irr} (L)$ supercuspidal, the function 
    $$\chi \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto W_{f, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \chi)}^1\vert_{P_n}$$
    is regular. In particular, the following conditions are satisfied.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[-]  For all $p \in P_n$, the function 
        $$\chi \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto W_{f, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \chi)}^1(p)$$
        is regular.
        \item[-] Thanks to Proposition \ref{Wpi}, if a pair $(L', \rho' \otimes \chi')$ is conjugated to $(L, \rho \otimes \chi)$, then 
        $$W_{f, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \chi)}^1 = W_{f, i_{Q'}^G(\rho'\otimes \chi')}^1.$$
    \end{enumerate}
    In other words, for all $p\in P_n$, $ev_p(V)$ is an ideal of $X'$, and for all $\chi \in \mathcal{X}(L)/W(L,\rho)$, 
    $$\mathrm{sp}_\chi(W_{f, \pi_{X'}}^1) = W_{f, \pi\otimes \chi}^1 \not = 0 $$
    for some $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, meaning that $V$ is included in none of the maximal ideals of $X'$. Hence, for all $p\in P_n$, 
    $$ev_p(V) = \{W_{f, \pi_{X'}}^1(p), \ f \in C_c^\infty(G)\}=X'.$$
    Applying now Lemma \ref{GKfam}, we obtain 
    $$C_c^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n, X', \psi_n) \subset \left\{W_{f, \pi_{X'}}^1 \vert_{P_n}, \ f \in C_c^\infty(G)\right\}$$
    and hence, there exists a function $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, such that 
    $$W_{f, \pi_{X'}}^1 \in C_c^\infty(N_n\backslash P_n, X', \psi_n).$$

title: Definition
body_md:
A regular section
    $$\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto W_\mu \in \mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \psi_n) ,$$
    is the composition of a regular section
    $$\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto e_\mu \in i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu),$$
    and the Jacquet functional $\Tilde{J}_{\rho\otimes \mu}^{\psi_n}$.

label: BetaFam
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{BetaFam}
    Let $\phi \in C_c^\infty(F^n)$. Suppose $\rho$ is supercuspidal or induced by an irreducible and supercuspidal representation. Then, for every regular section 
    $$\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto W_\mu \in \mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \psi_n) ,$$
    the function $\mu \in \mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{unit}}(L) \mapsto \beta^\rho_\mu(W_\mu\otimes \phi)$ extends to a rational function on $\mathcal{X}(L)$, such that 
    $$\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto \frac{\beta^\rho_\mu(W_\mu\otimes \phi)}{L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+)}$$
    is a regular function on $\mathcal{X}(L)$.
