title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{D}$ be an algebraic variety over $\mathbb{C}$. Let $V$ be a complex vector space of countable dimension, $\Tilde{V}$ its linear dual, and 
    $$x_r \in V \otimes \mathbb{C}[\mathcal{D}], \ \ c_r\in\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{D}], \ \ r\in R$$
    with $R$ a set of indexes. Let $\mathcal{U}\subseteq \mathcal{D}$ be open (for the analytic topology) and non-empty. Suppose that for all $d\in \mathcal{U}$, the system 
    $$\lambda (x_r(d)) = c_r(d)$$
    admits a unique solution $\lambda_d\in \Tilde{V}$. Then for all $v\in V$, there exists a non-empty, Zariski-open subset $\mathcal{V}\subseteq \mathcal{D}$ such that the function 
    $$d\in \mathcal{V}\cap \mathcal{D} \mapsto \lambda_d(v)$$
    extends to a regular function on $\mathcal{V}$. In particular, it defines a rational function on $\mathcal{D}$.
head: environment
name: Bernstein

title: Proof
body_md:
First of all, if $\rho=i_P^L(\sigma)$ with $P=M_PU_P$ a parabolic subgroup of $L$ and $\sigma\in \mathrm{Irr}(M_P)$ supercuspidal, then 
    $$i_Q^G(\rho \otimes \mu) \cong i_{P}^G(\sigma \otimes \mu\vert_{M_P}).$$
    This implies that, up to replacing $\beta_\mu^\rho$ by $\beta_\mu^\sigma$, we can assume that $\rho$ is supercuspidal.
    
    
    Using the notation of Bernstein's theorem, set $\mathcal{D}= \mathcal{X}(L)$. For all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L)$, denote $\pi_\mu = i_Q^G(\rho \otimes \mu)$ and $\omega_{\pi_\mu}=\omega_\rho \otimes \mu\vert_{Z_G}$ its central character. Let $K_0$ be a maximal compact subgroup of $G$, recall that for all $\mu\in \mathcal{X}(L)$, $\pi_\mu$ is isomorphic to $ i_{Q\cap K_0}^{K_0}(\rho\vert_{L\cap K_0})$ as a vector space, set 
    $$V= i_{Q\cap K_0}^{K_0}(\rho\vert_{L\cap K_0}) \otimes C_c^\infty(F^n).$$
    We first remark that, for all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{unit}}(L)$
    $$\beta_\mu^\rho \in \mathrm{Hom}_{G_n(F)}(\pi_\mu \otimes C_c^\infty(F^n), \vert \det \vert_F^{-1}).$$
    From now on, we follow and adapt the proof of Theorem 1 in \cite{Kab}, to show that the space $\mathrm{Hom}_{G_n(F)}(\pi_\mu \otimes C_c^\infty(F^n), \vert \det \vert_F^{-1})$ is at most one-dimensional for $\mu$ in a non-empty Zariski-open subset of $\mathcal{X}(L)$. Let $H=G_n(F)$, the short exact sequence of $H$-representation,
    $$0 \longrightarrow C_c^\infty(F^n\backslash\{0\}) \longrightarrow C_c^\infty(F^n) \longrightarrow \mathbb{C} \to 0$$
    induces an exact sequence
    $$0 \to \mathrm{Hom}_H(\pi_\mu, \vert \det \vert_F^{-1}) \to \mathrm{Hom}_H(\pi_\mu \otimes C_c^\infty(F^n), \vert \det \vert_F^{-1}) \to \mathrm{Hom}_H(\pi_\mu \otimes C_c^\infty(F^n\backslash\{0\}), \vert \det \vert_F^{-1}).$$
    For all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L)$, such that 
    $$\mu\vert_{Z_H} \not = \vert \det \vert_F^{-1}\otimes \omega_\rho\vert_{F^\times}^{-1}$$
    we have
    $$\mathrm{Hom}_H(\pi_\mu, \vert \det \vert_F^{-1})  = 0.$$
    The set
    $$\mathcal{U}_0=\{\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L), \ \mu\vert_{Z_H} \not = \vert \det \vert_F^{-1}\otimes \omega_\rho\vert_{F^\times}^{-1}\}$$
    is Zariski-open. Moreover, 
    \begin{align*}
        \mathrm{Hom}_H(\pi_\mu \otimes C_c^\infty(F^n\backslash\{0\}), \vert \det \vert_F^{-1}) & \cong \mathrm{Hom}_H(\pi_\mu , i_{P_n(F)}^H(\mathbf{1})), \\
        & \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{P_n(F)}(\pi_\mu, \mathbf{1}).
    \end{align*}
    where $\mathbf{1}$ denotes the trivial character of $P_n(F)$. Let $\mu \in \mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{unit}}(L)$. Denote by
    $$\mathbf{\Psi}^- : \mathrm{Rep}(P_n(E)) \to \mathrm{Rep}(G_{n-1}(E)) \ , \ \mathbf{\Psi}^+:\mathrm{Rep}(G_{n-1}(E)) \to \mathrm{Rep}(P_{n}(E)) $$ 
    and 
    $$\mathbf{\Phi}^- : \mathrm{Rep}(P_n(E)) \to \mathrm{Rep}(P_{n-1}(E)) \ , \ \mathbf{\Phi}^+:\mathrm{Rep}(P_{n-1}(E)) \to \mathrm{Rep}(P_{n}(E))$$
    the derivative functors defined by \cite{BZ1} in Section 3. Using the results in Section 3.5 of \cite{BZ1}, $\pi_\mu$ as a representation of $P_n(E)$, $\pi_\mu$ admits a filtration 
    $$0=\pi_{n+1} \subset \pi_n \subset \cdots \subset \pi_2 \subset \pi_1 = \pi_\mu,$$
    such that, for all $j \in \{1, \dots , n\}$
    $$\pi_j/ \pi_{j+1} \cong \mathbf{\Phi}^{j-1} \circ \mathbf{\Psi}^+(\pi^{(j)}),$$
    where $\pi^{(j)}$ denotes the j-th derivative. Let us show that the natural map
    $$\mathrm{Hom}_{P_n(F)}(\pi_\mu, \mathbf{1}) \to \mathrm{Hom}_{P_n(F)}(\pi_n, \mathbf{1})$$
    is injective for $\mu$ in general position. Indeed, let $T$ be an element in the kernel of the above map. If $T$ is non-zero, then there exists $j \in \{1, \dots, n-1\}$ such that
    $$T \vert_{\pi_j} \not = 0, \ \mathrm{but} \ T\vert_{\pi_{j+1}} = 0.$$
    Hence, $T$ induces a non trivial element in 
    $$\mathrm{Hom}_{P_n(F)}(\pi_j/\pi_{j+1}, \mathbf{1}).$$
    Applying repeatedly Proposition 1 in \cite{Kab}, we obtain 
    $$\mathrm{Hom}_{P_n(F)}(\pi_j/\pi_{j+1}, \mathbf{1}) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{P_{n-j+1}(F)}(\mathbf{\Psi}^+(\pi^{(j)}), \mathbf{1}).$$
    By definition of $\mathbf{\Psi}^+$ (Section 3.1, \cite{BZ1}), it is also isomorphic to 
    $$\mathrm{Hom}_{G_{n-j}(F)}(\pi^{(j)}, \mathbf{1}).$$

    We define 

    $$U_j := \begin{pmatrix}
        I_{n-j} & * \\ & N_j
    \end{pmatrix},$$
    and we see $\psi_j$ as a character of $U_j$ by composing with the projection from $U_j$ to $N_j$. The twisted Jacquet module 
    $$\pi_{U_j, \psi_j}= \mathbf{j}_{\psi_j}(\pi_\mu) =  \pi_\mu/\pi_\mu(U_j, \psi_j)$$
    is isomorphic to $\pi^{(j)}$. Set 
    $$V_j = \begin{pmatrix}
        I_{n-j} & * \\
         & I_j
    \end{pmatrix}.$$
    We also have 
    $$\pi^{(j)}\cong \mathbf{j}_{\psi_{j}}(\pi_{V_j}) = (\pi_{V_j})_{N_{j}, \psi_{j}}.$$
    Thanks to the geometric lemma \cite{Ren}, VI.5.1, the representation $\pi_{V_j}$ admits a filtration such that each subquotient admits a central character for the Levi $G_{n-j}(E)\times G_j(E)$. We denote by $\mathcal{W}_j$ a set of representative of the double cosets $Q\backslash G /Q'$, where $Q'$ is the parabolic subgroup with Levi $L_j=G_{n-j}(E)\times G_j(E)$ and unipotent radical $V_j$. Suppose $L=G_{n_1}(E)\times \cdots \times G_{n_k}(E)$. We identify $\mathcal{W}_j$ with the set of partitions $I_1\sqcup I_2 =\{1, \dots, k \}$ such that
    $$\sum_{i\in I_1}n_i=n-j, \ \mathrm{and } \ \sum_{i\in I_2}n_i=j,$$
    and for all $w\in \mathcal{W}_j$ we have
    $$w^{-1}Lw = \prod_{i\in I_1}G_{n_i}(E)\times \prod_{i\in I_2}G_{n_i}(E).$$
    Since $\rho$ is supercuspidal, the irreducible subquotients of $\pi_{V_j}$ arising from the geometric lemma are of the form 
    $$i_{L_j\cap w^{-1}Lw}^{L_j}\left(\rho\otimes \mu \right)^w, \  w \in \mathcal{W}_j$$
    We denote by 
    $$\omega_\rho \otimes \mu\vert_{Z_L} = (\omega_1 \mu_1, \dots, \omega_k \mu_k): (E^\times)^k \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}^\times$$
    the central character of $\rho\otimes\mu$. Therefore, the central characters of the irreducible subquotients of $\pi_{V_j}$ are characters of $E^\times \times E^\times$ of the form
    $$(\omega_\rho \otimes \mu\vert_{Z_L})^w = \left(\prod_{i\in I_1}\omega_{i} \mu_{i},\prod_{i\in I_2}\omega_{i} \mu_{i}\right), \ w \in \mathcal{W}_j.$$
    The central characters of $\pi^{(j)}$ correspond to the first entry
    $$\prod_{i\in I_1}\omega_{i} \mu_{i}.$$

    \bigskip 
    
    For all $w \in \mathcal{W}_{j}$, we denote by $\mathcal{U}_w$ the Zariski-open set of $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L)$, such that 
    $$\prod_{i\in I_1}\mu_{i}\vert_{F^\times} \not = \left(\prod_{i\in I_1}\omega_{i}\vert_{F^\times}\right)^{-1}.$$
    Then for all $\mu\in \bigcup_{w\in \mathcal{W}_{j}} \mathcal{U}_w$, we have 
    $$\mathrm{Hom}_{G_{n-j}(F)}(\pi^{(j)}, \mathbf{1})=0.$$
    which establish the injectivity of the map 
    $$\mathrm{Hom}_{P_n(F)}(\pi_\mu, \mathbf{1}) \to \mathrm{Hom}_{P_n(F)}(\pi_n, \mathbf{1}).$$
    Using again Proposition 1 in \cite{Kab} and the definition of $\mathbf{\Psi}^+$,
    $$\mathrm{Hom}_{P_n(F)}(\pi_n, \mathbf{1}) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{G_0(F)}(\pi^{(n)}, \mathbf{1}).$$
    The dimension of this last homomorphism space is one because it is the dimension of $\pi^{(n)}$, as $G_0(F)$ is the trivial group. Consequently, the space $\mathrm{Hom}_{P_n(F)}(\pi_\mu, \mathbf{1})$ and hence, the space 
    $$\mathrm{Hom}_{G_n(F)}(\pi_\mu \otimes C_c^\infty(F^n), \vert \det \vert_F^{-1}),$$
    are at most one-dimensional.
    
    Returning to the proof of the lemma, denote by $\mathcal{B}$ a basis of the vector space $V$. For all $e\otimes \phi \in \mathcal{B}$ there exists a compact-open subgroup $K_e\subset K_0$ of $G$, such that 
    $e \in \pi_\mu^{K_e}$, and $ H/(H\cap K_e)$ is a countable set, denote 
    $$R = \{(e \otimes \phi, h): \ e\otimes \phi \in \mathcal{B}, \ h \in H/(H\cap K_e)\}.$$ 
    Set $x_{(e \otimes \phi, h)}(\mu) = \pi_\mu(h)e \otimes R(h)\phi-\vert \det h\vert_F^{-1}.e \otimes \phi$. We have $x_{(e \otimes \phi, h)} \in V \otimes \mathbb{C}[\mathcal{D}]$. For all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{unit}}(L)$, the system
    $$L_\mu(x_{(e \otimes \phi, h)}(\mu) ) =0, \ (e \otimes \phi, h) \in R, \ L_\mu \in \Tilde{V}$$
    admits $\alpha\beta_\mu^\rho$ as solutions, with $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}$. In order to apply Bernstein's theorem we add another equation to system, to obtain $\beta_\mu^\rho$ as the unique solution. 
    
    Let $f \in C_c^\infty(N_n(E)\backslash P_n(E), \mathbb{C}[\mathcal{D}], \psi_n)$, such that
    $$\int_{N_n(F)\backslash P_n(F)}f(p)dp \not = 0.$$
    Thanks to Corollary \ref{CoroGKfamKirrilov}, there exists a regular section 
    $$e': \mu \in \mathcal{D}\mapsto e'(\mu) \in i_{Q \cap K_0}^{K_0}(\rho)^J,$$
    with $J$ a compact-open subgroup of $G$, such that
    $$W_{e'(\mu)}\vert_{P_n(E)} = \mathrm{sp}_\mu(f).$$
    Choosing $\phi'\in C_c^\infty(F^n)$ with support in $e_n(J \cap H)$, with $e_n = (0, \dots, 0, 1)$, and such that $\phi'(0)\not = 0$, we then have 
    $$Z(1, W_{e'(\mu)}, \phi') = \phi'(0) \int_{N_n(F)\backslash P_n(F)}W_{e'(\mu)}(p) dp \not = 0$$
    convergent for all $\mu \in \mathcal{D}$. Hence, 
    $$\mu \mapsto Z(1, W_{e'(\mu)}, \phi') \in \mathbb{C}[\mathcal{D}].$$  
    For all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{unit}}(L)$, the system 
    $$L_\mu(x_{(e \otimes \phi, h)}(\mu) ) =0, \ (e \otimes \phi, h) \in R,$$
    $$L_\mu(e'(\mu)\otimes \phi') = Z(1, W_{e'(\mu)}, \phi')$$
    admits a unique solution, $\beta_\mu^\rho$. Applying Bernstein's theorem, with $\mathcal{U}$ be the open set defined by the intersection 
    $$\mathcal{U} = \mathcal{U}_0\cap (\bigcup_{w\in \mathcal{W}_{j}}\mathcal{U}_w)\cap\left\{\mu=(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_k)\in \mathcal{X}(L), \ \Re(\mu_i)>-\frac{1}{2}\right\},$$
    we obtain that for every regular section $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto W_\mu$,
    $$(\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto \beta_\mu^\rho(W_\mu\otimes \phi')) \in \mathbb{C}(\mathcal{X}(L)).$$
    It remains to show that 
    $$\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto \frac{\beta^\rho_\mu(W_\mu\otimes \phi')}{L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+)}$$
    is a regular function on $\mathcal{X}(L)$. To do so, we use the following lemma.
    
    \begin{lem}
        Let $X$ be a complex, affine, irreducible and normal algebraic variety. We denote by $\mathbb{C}[X]$ the algebra of regular functions on $X$ and $\mathbb{C}(X)$ its field of fractions. Let $(\Delta_x)_{x\in X}$ be a family of closed and irreducible subvarieties of $X$, all of dimension one such that $x\in \Delta_x$, for all $x\in X$. If $f\in \mathbb{C}(X)$ is such that for all $x\in X$, none of the polar divisors of $f$ contains $\Delta_x$ and $f\vert_{\Delta_x}\in \mathbb{C}[\Delta_x]$, then $f\in \mathbb{C}[X]$.
    \end{lem}

    \begin{proof}
        For any prime ideal $P$ of $\mathbb{C}[X]$ denote by $V(P)$ the subvariety associated to $P$. Let $P$ be a prime ideal such that $V(P)$ is of codimension 1, the localization by $P$ is denoted by
        $$\mathbb{C}[X]_P=(\mathbb{C}[X]\backslash P)^{-1}.\mathbb{C}[X]\subset \mathbb{C}(X).$$
        Since $X$ is normal, we have 
        $$\mathbb{C}[X] = \bigcap_{P} \mathbb{C}[X]_P,$$
        where $P$ ranges over prime ideals of height one. Therefore it suffices to show that for all prime ideal $P$ of height one, 
        $$f\in \mathbb{C}[X]_P.$$
        Let $U_f=X \backslash \overline{\{x \in X, \ f(x)=0\}}$ be the fundamental open set associated to $f$. Let $P$ be a prime ideal of $\mathbb{C}[X]$, with $V(P)$ of codimension 1, such that $v_P(f)<0$. Let $x\in V(P) \cap U_f$, and $m_x\subset \mathbb{C}[X]$ the prime ideal corresponding to $x$, then we have $P\subset m_x$ and $P_x\subset m_x$ with $P_x$ the prime ideal corresponding to $\Delta_x$. Let $g=f^{-1}$, we then have $g(x)=0$, and we show that $g\vert_{\Delta_x}(x)=0$. As $x\in V(P) \cap U_f$, we have $g(x)=0$, or equivalently $g\in m_x.\mathbb{C}[X]_{m_x}$ (the unique maximal ideal of $\mathbb{C}[X]_{m_x}$). We have a projection 
        $$ \mathbb{C}[X]_{P_x} \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}[X]_{P_x}/P_x.\mathbb{C}[X]_{P_x} = \mathbb{C}(\Delta_x).$$
        And $m_x.\mathbb{C}[X]_{m_x}\subset \mathbb{C}[X]_{P_x}$. We denote $\overline{m_x}= m_x/P_x$ the maximal ideal corresponding to $x$ in $\mathbb{C}[\Delta_x]=\mathbb{C}[X]/P_x$. We have $\overline{m_x}.\mathbb{C}[\Delta_x]_{\overline{m_x}}\subset \mathbb{C}(\Delta_x)$, and this ideal is the image of $m_x.\mathbb{C}[X]_{m_x}$ by the above projection. We deduce that $g\vert_{\Delta_x}(x)=0$ and hence that $g\vert_{\Delta_x}\in \mathbb{C}[\Delta_x]_{\overline{m_x}}\backslash \mathbb{C}[\Delta_x]_{\overline{m_x}}^\times$. As $\mathbb{C}[\Delta_x]_{\overline{m_x}}$ is a local and integral ring, we have $g^{-1}=f\not \in\mathbb{C}[\Delta_x]_{\overline{m_x}}$, which means that $f$ has a pole in $\Delta_x$ and this contradicts the hypothesis $f\vert_{\Delta_x}\in \mathbb{C}[\Delta_x]$.
    \end{proof}
    We apply this lemma, with $\Delta_\mu=\{\mu_s= \mu \otimes \vert \det \vert_E^s, \ s \in \mathbb{C}\}$, for all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L)$. Recall that 
    $$i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu_s) \cong i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)\otimes \vert\det\vert_E^s.$$
    Hence,
    $$\mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu_s), \psi_n) \cong \mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \psi_n)\otimes \vert \det \vert_E^s,$$
    implying that $W_{\mu_s}$ can be written $\vert \det \vert_E^sW_{\mu, s}$ with $W_{\mu, s}\in \mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \psi_n)$. Remark that for all $s \in \mathbb{C}$
    $$\frac{\beta^\rho_{\mu_s}(\vert\det\vert_E^sW_{\mu,s}\otimes \phi)}{L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu_s), \mathrm{As}^+)}= \frac{Z(1+2s, W_{\mu,s}, \phi)}{L(1+2s, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+)}$$
    is indeed regular. This means that to show the regularity of the function 
    $$\mu_s \in \Delta_\mu \mapsto \frac{\beta^\rho_{\mu_s}(W_{\mu_s}\otimes \phi)}{L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu_s), \mathrm{As}^+)}$$
    it suffices to show that 
    $$s \in \mathbb{C} \mapsto\frac{Z(s, W_{\mu,s}, \phi)}{L(s, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+)}$$
    is regular. Since 
    $$s\in \mathbb{C}\mapsto W_{\mu,s}\in \mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes\mu), \psi_n)$$ 
    is a regular section, there exists a compact-open subgroup $K$ of $G$ such that for all $s\in \mathbb{C}$, 
    $$W_{\mu, s}\in \mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \psi_n)^K.$$
    Therefore, there exists a basis $\mathcal{B}_K$ of $ \mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \psi_n)^K$ such that $W_{\mu,s}$ can be written as a linear combination
    $$W_{\mu,s} = \sum_{W \in \mathcal{B}_K}\lambda_W(s)W,$$
    with $s\mapsto \lambda_W(s)$ a regular function. Finally, by definition of the Asai $L$-function the function 
    $$s \in \mathbb{C} \mapsto\frac{Z(s, W_{\mu,s}, \phi)}{L(s, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+)}$$
    is indeed regular.

title: Proof
body_md:
To simplify the notation, for all integers $r$, set $G_r=\mathrm{GL}_r(E)$ and $H_r=\mathrm{GL}_r(F)$.
  Write $L = G_{n_1}\times \cdots \times G_{n_k}$, with $(n_1, \dots, n_k)$ a partition of $n$, and 
  $$\rho\otimes \lambda = \rho_1\vert\det\vert_E^{\lambda_1} \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \rho_k\vert\det\vert_E^{\lambda_k}$$
  with $\rho_i$ irreducible unitary and supercuspidal and $\lambda_i\in \mathbb{R}$. Let $\{\mu_1, \dots, \mu_l\}$ be the set of distinct elements of $\{\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\}$, hence $\mu_1<\cdots<\mu_l$. For all $j\in \{1, \dots, l\}$, we define 
  $$\Sigma_j = \mathop{\vcenter{\hbox{\Large$\times$}}}\displaylimits_{\underset{\lambda_i = \mu_j}{1\leq i\leq k,}} \rho_{i} \in \mathrm{Irr} (G_{\sum n_{i,j}})$$
  where $n_{i,j} = n_j$ if $\lambda_j=\lambda_i$ (otherwise $n_{i,j}=0$); so that 
  $$i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \lambda) = i_{Q'}^G(\Sigma_1\vert \det\vert^{\mu_1}\boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \Sigma_l\vert \det\vert^{\mu_l})  $$
  with $\mu_1<\cdots<\mu_l$, and $Q' = MU'$ the standard parabolic subgroup such that 
  $$M = G_{d_1}\times \cdots \times G_{d_l}, \ \mathrm{with} \ \  d_i =\sum_{j=1}^k n_{i,j}.$$ 

  We now use Proposition 5.4 of \cite{LgeoMatringe}. Following this paper, we parametrize the double cosets in $Q'\backslash G/H$ by symmetric matrices $a=(a_{i,j})_{i,j}$ of size $l$ and with non-negative integer coefficients, such that for all $i\in \{1, \dots, l\}$, $\sum_{j=1}^la_{i,j}=d_i$. Every line of the matrix $a$ defines a partition of $d_i$, and we set 
  $$M_u=M_{u,1}\times \cdots \times M_{u,l},$$
  where each $M_{u,i} = G_{a_{i,1}}\times \cdots \times G_{a_{i,l}}$ is a Levi subgroup of $G_{d_i}$. Again, according to \cite{LgeoMatringe}, we let $M_u^u$ be the subgroup

  $$M_u^u= \prod_{i=1}^lH_{a_{i,i}}\times \prod_{i<j}G_{a_{i,j}}$$
  embedded in $M_u$ through the map that sends an element $((h_i)_{i=1}^l, (g_{i,j})_{i<j})\in M_u^u$ to the element $m \in M_u$ whose coordinates verify
  $$ m_{i,j} = \left\{\begin{array}{cc}
       h_i, &  \mathrm{if} \ i=j\\
       g_{i,j}, & \mathrm{if} \ i<j \\
       g_{i,j}^c, & \mathrm{if} \ i>j
  \end{array}\right.$$
  The geometric lemma, proposition 5.4 of \cite{LgeoMatringe}, provides an injection of $\mathrm{Hom}_H(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \lambda), \mathbb{C})$ into 
  $$\prod_{u\in Q'\backslash G/H} \mathrm{Hom}_{M_u^u}(r_{M_u}^M(\Sigma_1\vert \det\vert^{\mu_1}\boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \Sigma_l\vert \det\vert^{\mu_l}), \mathbb{C}).$$
                         
                                                                                                                                                
  We parametrize the real unramified characters of $M_u$ by 
  $$\bigoplus_{\underset{a_{i,j \not = 0}}{1\leq i,j \leq l}}\mathbb{R},$$
  where $\lambda = (\lambda_{i,j})_{1\leq i,j \leq l}$ corresponds to the character
  $$(g_{i,j}) \in M_u \mapsto \prod_{i,j}\vert \det g_{i,j}\vert^{\lambda_{i,j}}.$$
  Lemma \ref{expUnit} implies that the real part of the exponents of $r_{M_u}^M(\Sigma_1\vert \det\vert^{\mu_1}\boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \Sigma_l\vert \det\vert^{\mu_l})$ is of the form $(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_1, \mu_2, \dots, \mu_2, \dots, \mu_l, \dots, \mu_l)$ (each $\mu_i$ appearing $l$ times). Suppose that 
  $$\mathrm{Hom}_{M_u^u}(r_{M_u}^M(\Sigma_1\vert \det\vert^{\mu_1}\boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \Sigma_l\vert \det\vert^{\mu_l}), \mathbb{C}) \not =0.$$
  Then, in particular, the restriction to $M_u^u$ of the exponents of $r_{M_u}^M(\Sigma_1\vert \det\vert^{\mu_1}\boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \Sigma_l\vert \det\vert^{\mu_l})$ should be trivial.  So, if there exists an index $i$ such that $a_{i,i}\not = 0$, we get $\mu_i = 0$. As all the $\mu_i$'s are different, if this $i$ exists, it is unique. Moreover, if for $i\not =j$, we have $a_{i,j}\not = 0$ then $\mu_i+\mu_j=0$. Hence, the only double coset $u \in Q' \backslash G /H$, for which the space $\mathrm{Hom}_{M_u^u}(r_{M_u}^M(\Sigma_1\vert \det\vert^{\mu_1}\boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \Sigma_l\vert \det\vert^{\mu_l}), \mathbb{C})$ can possibly be non zero, is the one corresponding to the matrix 
  $$a = \begin{pmatrix}
        0 & \cdots & d_1 \\
          & \mathinner
{\mkern1mu\raise1pt\vbox{\kern7pt\hbox{.}}
\mkern2mu\raise4pt\hbox{.}
\mkern2mu\raise7pt\hbox{.}\mkern1mu} & \\
        d_l & \cdots & 0  
    \end{pmatrix}$$
  which implies in particular $d_i = d_{l-i+1}$, for all $i$. For all $i$, denote by $G_{d_i}^{\mathrm{diag^c}}$ the subgroup consisting of elements $(g, g^c)$, with $g\in G_{d_i}$. Denote $\alpha=\lfloor l/2\rfloor+1$ if $l$ is odd, $\alpha=0$ if $l$ is even. It remains to show that the space 
  $$\mathrm{Hom}_{M^u}(\Sigma_1\vert \det\vert^{\mu_1}\boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \Sigma_l\vert \det\vert^{\mu_l}, \mathbb{C}) = \mathrm{Hom}_{H_{d_\alpha}} (\Sigma_\alpha, \mathbb{C}) \otimes \bigotimes_{i=1}^{\lfloor l/2\rfloor} \mathrm{Hom}_{G_{d_i}^{\mathrm{diag}^c}}(\Sigma_i\vert \det\vert^{\mu_i}\boxtimes \Sigma_{l-i+1}\vert \det\vert^{-\mu_i}, \mathbb{C})$$
  is at most one-dimensional. We first remark that if $\alpha \not = 0$, then
  $$\mathrm{Hom}_{H_{d_\alpha}}(\Sigma_\alpha, \mathbb{C})$$
  is known to be at most one-dimensional. Finally, the space
  $$\mathrm{Hom}_{G_{d_i}^{\mathrm{diag^c}}}(\Sigma_i\vert \det\vert^{\mu_i}\boxtimes \Sigma_{l-i+1}\vert \det\vert^{-\mu_i}, \mathbb{C})$$
  is non zero if and only if $\Sigma_i \cong \Sigma_{l-i+1}^*$ and in that case the dimension is one.

\begin{lem}\label{RestReg}
    Let $\Phi : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be a meromorphic function and let $V, \Delta$ be vector subspaces of $\mathbb{C}^n$, with $\dim \Delta = 1$. Suppose the following conditions.
    \begin{enumerate}
    
        \item The restriction $\Phi\vert_V$ is well defined as a meromorphic function. In other words, $V$ is not included in any of the poles of $\Phi$.
        \item For all $v\in V$, the restriction $\Phi\vert_{v+\Delta}$ is well defined as a meromorphic function and is regular in $v$.
        \item The poles $D_1, \dots, D_m$ of $\Phi$ are all simple and affine hyperplanes, and for all $i\not= j $
        $$D_i \cap V \not = D_j \cap V.$$
        
    \end{enumerate}

    Then $\Phi\vert_V$ is holomorphic on $V$.
\end{lem}

\begin{proof}
    First, remark that, since for all $i\not = j$, 
    $$D_i \cap V \not = D_j \cap V,$$
    the codimension of $D_i\cap V \cap D_j$ in $V$ is either $2$ or $\infty$. Therefore, applying Hartogs' lemma, it suffices to show that for all $v\in D_i\cap V\backslash (\bigcup_{i\not = j}D_i\cap D_j\cap V)$, the function $\Phi\vert _V$ is holomorphic in a neighborhood of $v$. Let $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, for simplicity, denote $D=D_i$. Let $v\in D\cap V\backslash (\bigcup_{i\not = j}D_i\cap D_j\cap V)$, there exists an open neighborhood $U_v$ of $v$, such that we can write 
    $$\Phi\vert_{U_v} = \frac{g}{\lambda},$$
    where $\lambda$ denotes an equation of the hyperplane $D$ and $g$ is a holomorphic function in $U_v$. Without loss of generality, we can choose a system of coordinates such that $D$ is the set of elements $z= (z_1, \dots, z_n)\in \mathbb{C}^n$, such that $z_1=0$. Hence, it suffices to show that the function 
    $$z= (z_1, \dots, z_n) \in U_v\cap V \mapsto \Phi(z) = \frac{g(z)}{z_1},$$
    is holomorphic, or equivalently, that $g=0$ on $U_v\cap V\cap D$. By Assumption 1, we have 
    $$V \not \subseteq D = \{z=(z_1, \cdots, z_n)\in \mathbb{C}^n, \ z_1=0\}.$$
    By Assumption 2, for all $z\in V$ the function
    $$\alpha \in \mathbb{C}\mapsto\Phi(z+\alpha l), \ l \in \Delta$$
    is holomorphic at $\alpha=0$. Hence, for $z\in U_v\cap V\cap D$
    $$\alpha \mapsto\Phi(z+\alpha l) = \frac{g(z+\alpha l)}{\alpha l_1}$$
    is also holomorphic in $\alpha = 0$, meaning that $g(z) = 0$ for all $z\in U_v \cap V\cap D$ and that finishes the proof.
    
\end{proof}

We now want to apply this lemma to a meromorphic continuation of the relative characters given by a consequence of Proposition \ref{BetaFam}. We extend the definition of relative characters to $\mathrm{Temp}(G)$. Let $Q=LU$ be a parabolic subgroup of $G$, and let $\rho$ be a representation of $L$, induced from an irreducible and supercuspidal representation. We define, for all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{unit}}(L)$,
$$I_{i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)}(f) := \beta^{\rho}_\mu (W_{f,i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu) }^1)= \sum_{e\in \mathcal{B}({i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)})} \beta^{\rho}_\mu(R(f)e) J^\rho_\mu(e^\vee),$$
where $J^\rho_\mu$ denotes the the Jacquet functional on $i_Q^G(\rho^\vee\otimes -\mu)$.
\begin{coro}[of Proposition \ref{BetaFam}]
    Using the same notation, the function 
    $$\mu \in \mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{unit}}(L) \mapsto I_{i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)}(f)$$
    admits a meromorphic continuation to $\mathcal{X}(L)$. 
                                                                      
\end{coro}
Indeed, the meromorphic continuation is a direct consequence of Proposition \ref{BetaFam}, the regularity of Jacquet's functionals and the formula
$$I_{i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)}(f) = \beta^{\rho}_\mu (W_{f,i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu) }^1).$$
Denote by $\pi_\mu^+$ the unique irreducible and generic subquotient of $i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)$. Thanks to Proposition \ref{Wpi}, for all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L)$, we have 
$$W_{f, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)}^1 = W_{f, \pi_\mu^+}^1 \in \mathcal{W}(\pi_\mu^+, \psi_n).$$
Since two induced representations of the form 
$$i_Q^G(\rho), \ \ \mathrm{and} \ \ i_{Q'}^G(\rho')$$
have the same Jordan-Hölder factors as long as the cuspidal pairs $(L, \rho)$, $(L', \rho')$ are conjugate, the function $W_{f, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)}^1 = W_{f, \pi_\mu^+}^1$ only depends on the generic subquotient $\pi_\mu^+$, which does not depend on the choice of a parabolic. Therefore, the above definition of $I_{i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)}$ does not depend on the choice of the parabolic subgroup $Q$.


We now show that this rational extension of the relative characters is a regular function when restricted to the image of the base-change map. For $M$ a Levi subgroup of $U(n)$, and $\sigma$ an irreducible, unitary, and supercuspidal representation of $M$, assume $\rho = BC_n(\sigma)$ (is a representation of $L=\mathrm{Res}_{E/F}M_E(F)$), and $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(M)$. We identify 
$$\mathbb{C}^k \cong \mathfrak{a}_{L, \mathbb{C}}^* = X^*(L)\otimes \mathbb{C}.$$
We say that a character $\mu\in \mathfrak{a}^*_{L, \mathbb{C}}$ is \emph{anti-dominant} with respect to $Q=LU$ standard with $L=G_{n_1}\times \cdots \times G_{n_k}$, if $\mu=(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_k)$ with $\Re(\mu_1)\leq \cdots \leq \Re(\mu_k)$. Let 
$$\mu \in \mathfrak{a}_{L, \mathbb{C}}^*\mapsto e_\mu\in i_{Q}^G(\rho \otimes \mu)$$ 
be regular section and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(F^n)$. We apply Lemma \ref{RestReg} to 
$$\Phi :\mu \in \mathfrak{a}_{L, \mathbb{C}}^* \mapsto \beta_\mu^{\rho}(e_\mu \otimes \phi),$$ 
with $V=\mathfrak{a}_{M, \mathbb{C}}^*\subset \mathfrak{a}_{L, \mathbb{C}}^*$ and $\Delta = \{\vert \det \vert_E^s, \  s\in \mathbb{C}\}$, in order to show that $\Phi\vert_V$ is regular on 
$$V_Q^-:= \{\lambda \in V \  \mathrm{anti-dominant}\}.$$

By definition, 
$$\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto \beta_\mu^{BC_n(\sigma)}(e_\mu \otimes \phi)$$
is regular in a neighborhood of the unitary characters, in particular it is regular in a neighborhood of $0 \in \mathcal{X}(M)$, meaning that none of the poles contain $0$, therefore they do not contain $\mathcal{X}(M)$. 
                                                                                                                                            
In other words,
$$\Phi :\mu \in \mathfrak{a}_{L, \mathbb{C}}^* \mapsto \beta_\mu^{\rho}(e_\mu \otimes \phi),$$
is a meromorphic function verifying condition 1 of Lemma \ref{RestReg}. 

The second part of Proposition \ref{BetaFam} ensures that
$$\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto \frac{\beta^\rho_\mu(e_\mu \otimes \phi)}{L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+)}$$
is a regular function on $\mathcal{X}(L)$. In particular, in the proof we show that for all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L)$
$$s \in \Delta \mapsto \frac{\beta^\rho_{\mu_s}(e_{\mu_s} \otimes \phi)}{L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu_s), \mathrm{As}^+)},$$
where $\mu_s= \mu \otimes \vert \det \vert_E^s$, is regular, and therefore this also holds for all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(M)$. Recall that we have fixed the isomorphism between $i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)$ and its Whittaker model via the Jacquet functional. Since $W_{\mu_s} \in \mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu_s), \psi_n)$ can be written as $\vert \det \vert_E^sW_{\mu, s}$ with $W_{\mu, s}\in \mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \psi_n)$, we showed that the regularity of the above quotient is given by the regularity of 
$$s \in \mathbb{C} \mapsto\frac{Z(1+2s, W_{\mu,s}, \phi)}{L(1+2s, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+)}.$$
If $\mu$ is anti-dominant, then the unique generic irreducible subquotient $\pi_\mu^+$ of $i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)$ is in fact a quotient (see Proposition 2.10 in \cite{BZ2}, or \cite{JS}). In that case we have $W_{\mu,s} \in \mathcal{W}(\pi^+_\mu, \psi_n)$ and $Z(1+2s, W_{\mu,s}, \phi)$ is regular at $s=0$.

Combining Proposition 7.4 in \cite{GGPlocalroot} and Proposition \ref{LAd}, we obtain that 
$$L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+)\not = \infty,$$
as long as $i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)$ is irreducible. Recall that there exists a parabolic subgroup $Q'=L'U'$, a tempered irreducible representation $\rho'$ of $L'$ and a dominant character $\mu'\in \mathcal{X}(L')$ such that $\pi_\mu^+$ is isomorphic to its  standard module $i_{Q'}^G(\rho'\otimes \mu')$. Even if $\pi_\mu^+$ might not be in the image of the base-change map, it is a conjugate-dual representation. Indeed, $(\pi_\mu^+)^*$ is the unique generic irreducible subquotient of 
$$i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)^*\cong i_Q^G((\rho\otimes \mu)^*) \cong i_{\overline{Q}}^G(\rho\otimes \mu).$$
Therefore, 
$$\pi_\mu^+\cong(\pi_\mu^+)^*$$
and we can use again Proposition 7.4 in \cite{GGPlocalroot} and Proposition \ref{LAd}, to get
$$L(1, \pi_\mu^+, \mathrm{As}^+) = L(1, i_{Q'}^G(\rho'\otimes \mu'), \mathrm{As}^+) \not = \infty.$$
This shows that condition 2 of Lemma \ref{RestReg} is satisfied, with 
$$\Delta_\mu = \{\mu \otimes \vert \det \vert^s, s \in \mathbb{C}\}, \ \forall \mu \in V_{Q}^-.$$

It remains to show that the third condition is satisfied. Set
$$M = G_{m_1}\times \dots \times G_{m_r}\times U(l), \ \ \mathrm{and} \ \ \sigma = \sigma_1 \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \sigma_r \boxtimes \sigma^u$$
with $\sigma_i, \sigma^u$ irreducible, supercuspidal and unitary. Then 
$$\rho = \sigma_1 \boxtimes \sigma_1^* \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes \sigma_r \boxtimes \sigma_r^* \boxtimes BC_n(\sigma^u)$$
and we show that the poles of 
$$\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+)$$
are simple, defined by hyperplanes that are different when intersected with $\mathcal{X}(M)$. Recall that the Asai $L$-function decomposes as follows.
\begin{align*}
    L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+) = & \prod_{i=1}^rL(1+2\mu_i, \sigma_i, \mathrm{As}^+)L(1-2\mu_i, \sigma_i^*, \mathrm{As}^+) \\
    & \times L(1, BC_n(\sigma^u), \mathrm{As}^+) \times \prod_{i=1}^rL(1, \sigma_i\boxtimes\sigma_i^\vee) \\
    & \times \prod_{i<j} [ L(1+\mu_i+\mu_j, \sigma_i\boxtimes\sigma_j^c)L(1-\mu_i+\mu_j, \sigma_i^*\boxtimes\sigma_j^c) \\
    &  \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \    L(1+\mu_i-\mu_j, \sigma_i\boxtimes\sigma_j^\vee)L(1-\mu_i-\mu_j, \sigma_i^*\boxtimes\sigma_j^\vee) ] \\
    & \times \prod_{i=1}^r L(1+\mu_i, \sigma_i \boxtimes BC_n(\sigma^u)^c)L(1-\mu_i, \sigma_i^* \boxtimes BC_n(\sigma^u)^\vee)
\end{align*}
Note that we have 
$$\varphi =\left( \bigoplus_{i=1}^r \varphi_i \right) \oplus \varphi_{\sigma^u},$$
with $\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_r, \varphi_{\sigma^u}$ trivial on $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$. Thanks to Proposition \ref{propcuspBC}, we also have 
$$\varphi_{BC_n(\sigma^u)}= \bigoplus_{i=1}^{r'}\varphi'_i$$
conjugate-orthogonal, where $\varphi'_i$ is trivial on $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ and for all $i\not = j$, $\varphi'_i\not = \varphi_j'$. We first remark that we have 
$$L(1, BC_n(\sigma^u), \mathrm{As}^+)\not = \infty$$ because the representation $BC_n(\sigma^u)$ is tempered. For all $i\in \{1, \dots, r\}$, we have 
$$L(1, \sigma_i\boxtimes \sigma_i^\vee)=\infty$$
if and only if $\sigma_i \cong \vert \cdot \vert\sigma_i$ which never happens. The following list consists of the possible equations for the poles of the function 
$$\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L) \mapsto L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+).$$
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For all $i\in \{1, \dots, r\}$ the representation $\sigma_i$ is supercuspidal and unitary, hence $L(1+2\mu_i, \sigma_i, \mathrm{As}^+)$ has a pole if $1+2\mu_i \in i\mathbb{R}$, denote 
    $$D_1=\{\Re(\mu_i)=-1/2\}.$$
    \item Similarly, $L(1-2\mu_i, \sigma_i, \mathrm{As}^+)$ has a pole if $1-2\mu_i \in i\mathbb{R}$, denote 
    $$D_2= \{\Re(\mu_i)=1/2\}.$$
    \item For all $i<j$, $ L(1+\mu_i+\mu_j, \sigma_i\boxtimes\sigma_j^c)$ can have a pole on $1+\mu_i+\mu_j \in i \mathbb{R}$,
    $$D_3 = \{\Re(\mu_i) + \Re(\mu_j)=-1\}$$
    \item For all $i<j$, $ L(1-\mu_i+\mu_j, \sigma_i^*\boxtimes\sigma_j^c)$ can have a pole on $1-\mu_i+\mu_j \in i \mathbb{R}$,
    $$D_4 =\{\Re(\mu_i) - \Re(\mu_j)=1\} $$
    \item For all $i<j$, $ L(1+\mu_i-\mu_j, \sigma_i\boxtimes\sigma_j^\vee)$ can have a pole on $1+\mu_i-\mu_j \in i \mathbb{R}$,
    $$D_5 =\{\Re(\mu_i) - \Re(\mu_j)=-1\} $$
    \item For all $i<j$, $ L(1-\mu_i-\mu_j, \sigma_i^*\boxtimes\sigma_j^\vee)$ can have a pole on $1-\mu_i-\mu_j \in i \mathbb{R}$,
    $$D_6 =\{\Re(\mu_i) + \Re(\mu_j)=1\} $$
    \item Thanks to the decomposition of $\varphi_{BC_n(\sigma^u)}$ given above, $L(1+\mu_i, \sigma_i \boxtimes BC_n(\sigma^u)^c)$ has a pole for $1+\mu_i \in i\mathbb{R}$, denote 
    $$D_7= \{\Re(\mu_i)=-1\}.$$
    \item Similarly, $L(1-\mu_i, \sigma_i^* \boxtimes BC_n(\sigma^u)^\vee)$ has a pole for $1-\mu_i \in i\mathbb{R}$, denote 
    $$D_8= \{\Re(\mu_i)=1\}.$$
    
\end{enumerate}
Clearly, for all $i\not = j$, we have $D_i\not = D_j$, which means that the poles of $L(1, i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu), \mathrm{As}^+)$ for $\rho \otimes \mu = BC_n(\sigma_i)\otimes \mu$ with $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(M)$ are at most simple. It allows us to use Lemma \ref{RestReg}, and therefore the function 
$$\Phi :\mu \in \mathfrak{a}_{M, \mathbb{C}}^* \mapsto \beta_\mu^{\rho}(e_\mu \otimes \phi),$$
is regular for all $\mu$ anti-dominant. As a direct consequence, we obtain the regularity of 
$$\mu \in \mathcal{X}(M) \mapsto I_{i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)}(f) = \beta^{\rho}_\mu (W_{f,\pi_\mu^+ }^1)$$
for all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(M)$, since the definition of $I_{i_Q^G(\rho\otimes \mu)}(f)$ does not depend on the choice of $Q$.



         
          
                                                                     
                                               
                                                                                               
                  

Let $\lambda \in \mathcal{X}(M)$ be anti-dominant. Assume there exists a representation $\gamma\in \mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n))$, such that $BC_n(\gamma) = \pi_\lambda^+$, and 

$$\begin{array}{cccc}
     \beta_{\pi_\lambda^+} : & \pi_\lambda^+ & \to & \mathbb{C}  \\
     & v & \longmapsto & \beta(W_v)
\end{array}$$
and 
$$J_{\pi_\lambda^+} :  (\pi_\lambda^+)^\vee  \to  \mathbb{C}, $$
such that the relative character of $\pi_\lambda^+$ can be written as
$$I_{\pi_\lambda^+}(f) = \beta_{\pi_\lambda^+} (W_{f, \pi_\lambda^+}^1) = \sum_{v\in \mathcal{B}(\pi_\lambda^+)}\beta_{\pi_\lambda^+}(R(f)v).J_{\pi_\lambda^+}(v^\vee),$$
where $\mathcal{B}(\pi_\lambda^+)$ is an orthonormal basis of $\pi_\lambda^+$. Set $\beta_\lambda=\beta_\lambda^{BC_n(\sigma)} \in \mathrm{Hom}_H(i_Q^G(BC_n(\sigma) \otimes \lambda, \mathbb{C})$, we have the following diagrams. 

$$\xymatrix{
     i_Q^G(BC_n(\sigma)\otimes \lambda)  \ar[rd]_{\beta_\lambda} \ar[r]^{p}  & {\pi_\lambda^+}\ar[d]^{\beta_{\pi_\lambda^+}} \\
      & \mathbb{C}
     }$$
where $p$ is the natural projection. And

$$\xymatrix{
      ({\pi_\lambda^+})^\vee \ar[rd]_{J_{\pi_\lambda^+}} \ar[r]^{\iota}  &  i_Q^G(BC_n(\sigma)^\vee\otimes -\lambda) \ar[d]^{J_\lambda} \\
      & \mathbb{C}
     }$$
where $\iota$ is the natural injection, and by uniqueness of Whittaker functionals, $J_{\pi_\lambda^+}$ and $J_\lambda$ are proportional. We recall Proposition \ref{Wpi}, namely
$$W_{f, i_Q^G(BC_n(\sigma)\otimes \lambda)}^1 = W_{f, {\pi_\lambda^+}}^1 \in \mathcal{W}({\pi_\lambda^+}, \psi_n),$$
for all $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$. Moreover, thanks to Corollary \ref{CoroGKfam}, we can find a function $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$ such that 
$$\beta_\lambda(W_{f, i_Q^G(BC_n(\sigma)\otimes \lambda)}^1) = \beta_\lambda (W_{f, {\pi_\lambda^+}}^1) \not = 0,$$
Thus,
$$\mathrm{Hom}_H(i_Q^G(BC_n(\sigma)\otimes \lambda), \mathbb{C})\not = 0.$$

\begin{coro}[of Proposition \ref{BetaProportional}]
    Let $\gamma\in \mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n))$ be a subquotient of $i_P^{U(n)}(\sigma\otimes \lambda)$, where $P=MU$ is a parabolic subgroup of $U(n)$, $\sigma\in \mathrm{Irr} (M)$ supercuspidal and unitary and $\lambda\in \mathcal{X}(M)$ is real. Then, for all function $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, we have
    $$ I_{BC_n(\gamma)}(f) = I_{BC_n(i_P^{U(n)}(\sigma\otimes \lambda))}(f).$$
\end{coro}
Recall that we have defined 
$$BC_n(i_P^{U(n)}(\sigma\otimes\lambda)) = i_{Q}^G(BC_n(\sigma)\otimes \lambda).$$
We have shown in part \ref{cuspBC}, and more precisely in Proposition \ref{propcuspBC}, that the base-change of an irreducible supercuspidal and generic representation of a unitary group is an induced representation of supercuspidal representations in $G$. Hence, thanks to Proposition \ref{BetaProportional}, when $\lambda$ is anti-dominant with respect to $Q$, the space $\mathrm{Hom}_H(i_Q^G(BC_n(\sigma)\otimes \lambda), \mathbb{C})$ is at most one dimensional, implying that $\beta_\lambda$ and $\beta_{\pi_\lambda^+} \circ p$ are proportional, where $\pi_\lambda^+$ denotes $BC_n(\gamma)$. Therefore, there exists a constant $c\in \mathbb{C}$, such that the following equality holds for all $f \in C_c^\infty(G)$
$$\beta_{\pi_\lambda^+} =c.\beta_\lambda.$$
Thanks to Corollary \ref{CoroGKfamKirrilov}, we can chose a family $v_\mu\otimes \phi \in i_Q^G(BC_n(\sigma_X))\otimes C_c^\infty(F^n)$, with $\hat{\phi}(0)\not =0$ and the image $W_\mu\in \mathcal{W}(i_Q^G(BC_n(\sigma_X)), \psi_n)$ of the family $v_\mu$ is such that 
$$W_\mu \in C_c^\infty(N_n(E)\backslash P_n(E), X, \psi_n),$$
and
$$\int_{N_n(F)\backslash P_n(F)}W_\mu(p)dp \not = 0$$
converges for all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}(L)$. Since for all $\mu \in \mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{unit}}(L)$, we have 
$$\beta_\mu(v_\mu\otimes \phi) = \int_{N_n(F)\backslash P_n(F)}W_\mu(p)dp,$$
this formula extends to $\mathcal{X}(L)$ by analytic continuation. In particular, when $\mu = \lambda$, 
$$\beta_\lambda(v_\lambda\otimes \phi) = \int_{N_n(F)\backslash P_n(F)}W_\lambda(p)dp = \beta_{\pi_\lambda^+} \circ p (v_\lambda \otimes \phi).$$
Therefore $c = 1$, that is 
$$I_{{\pi_\lambda^+}}(f)= I_{BC_n(i_P^{U(n)}(\sigma\otimes \lambda))}(f).$$
We then have shown that
$$\{ \pi \in BC_n(\mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n))) \mapsto I_\pi(f), \ f\in C_c^\infty(G)\} \subseteq \mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{gen}}(U(n))\vert_{\mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n))}.$$
Finally, the action of $\mathfrak{Z}(G)$ on $C_c^\infty(G)$ gives rise to an action of $\mathfrak{Z}(G)$ on 
$$\{ \pi \in \mathrm{Temp}_H(G) \mapsto I_\pi(f), \ f\in C_c^\infty(G)\}$$
by $I_\pi(z.f)=z_\pi I_\pi(f)$, $z\in \mathfrak{Z}(G)$ where $z_\pi$ is a scalar. By the proposition \ref{closedim}, the surjection from $\mathfrak{Z}(G)$ to $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{gen}}(U(n))$ provides an action of $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{gen}}(U(n))$ on 
$$\{ \pi \in BC_n(\mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n)) \mapsto I_\pi(f), \ f\in C_c^\infty(G)\},$$
which makes it an ideal of $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{gen}}(U(n))$. The Corollary \ref{CoroGKfam} shows that 
$$\{ \pi \in BC_n(\mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n)) \mapsto I_\pi(f), \ f\in C_c^\infty(G)\}$$
is included in none of the maximal ideals of $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{gen}}(U(n))$ and hence 
$$\{ \pi \in BC_n(\mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n)) \mapsto I_\pi(f), \ f\in C_c^\infty(G)\}=\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathrm{gen}}(U(n))$$

Two functions $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, and $f'\in C_c^\infty(U(n))$ are \emph{transfers} from one to the other if for all $\pi\in \mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n))$
    $$I_{BC_n(\pi)}(f) = J_\pi(f').$$
head: environment
name: Spectral transfer

title: Example
body_md:
Let $w=w_n$ be the longest element in $W_{U(n)}$. For any $n\in N'$, the element $w_nnw_n^{-1}$ belongs to the unipotent radical of the opposite Borel subgroup, $\overline{N'}$, in particular for all $t\in T'$
    $$(N'\times N')_{tw_n} = \{(1,1)\}.$$
    Therefore, $N't\overset{.}{w_n} N'$ is always relevant, in other words
    $$T'w_n \subset N' \backslash U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}}/N'.$$
    Now let $w= 1$, for all $t\in T'$ and all $n\in N'$ we have $tnt^{-1}\in N$, i.e.
    $$(N'\times N')_t = \{(tnt^{-1}, n) \vert \ n\in N'\}.$$
    The corresponding double coset is relevant if and only if 
    $$\psi'(tnt^{-1}n^{-1}) = 1, \forall n\in N',$$
    if and only if $t\in Z_{U(n)}$. Since $\psi'$ is generic, by definition, $N'tN'$ with $t\in Z_{U(n)}$ is always relevant. In other words
    $$Z_{U(n)} \subset N' \backslash U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}}/N'.$$

label: Relelements
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Relelements}
Consider $G$ and the Borel subgroup $B=TN$ of upper triangular matrices. The Bruhat decomposition of $G$ can be written as 
$$G = NN_G(T)N, \ \mathrm{with} \ N_G(T) = T\rtimes W_G.$$
Define 
$$N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}:= N_G(T) \cap G_{rel}.$$
Let $g \in N_G(T) = T\rtimes W_G$. The stabilizer of $g$ is given by 
$$(N\times N)_g = \{ (n_1,n_2) \in N\times N \mid  n_1^{-1}gn_2=g \}.$$
We now follow the description of relevant elements, given by Jacquet-Ye \cite{JacquetYe}. Let $\theta_0:N\to E$ be an algebraic additive character defined by 

$$\theta_0\begin{pmatrix}
        1 & u_1 &  * & \dots  & * \\
          & \ddots & \ddots& \ddots  & \vdots \\
          & & \ddots & \ddots & * \\
          &  &  &\ddots &   u_{n-1} \\
          & & & & 1
    \end{pmatrix} = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}u_i,$$
and recall that $\psi = \psi_0\circ \theta_0$. An element $g'$ is \emph{Jacquet-Ye relevant} if the character $(n_1,n_2)\mapsto \theta_0 (n_1n_2)$ is trivial on the stabilizer
$$N^{g'}= \{(n_1,n_2) \in N\times N \mid {}^tn_1g'n_2=g'\}.$$
Since $\theta_0$ is an algebraic additive character, and $N^{g'}$ is connected, we have 
$$\theta_0(N^{g'}) = \{0\}, \ \mathrm{or} \ E.$$
Therefore, $\theta_0$ is trivial on $N^{g'}$, if and only if $\psi = \psi_0 \circ \theta_0$ is trivial on $N^{g'}$. Let $w_n = w_l^G$ be the longest element in $G$. For all $g\in G$, we have 
$$N^{w_ng} = (N\times N)_g,$$
because $(n_1,n_2)\in N^{w_ng}$, if and only if, $(w_n{}^tn_1^{-1}w_n, n_2)\in (N\times N)_g$. This shows that an element $g\in N_G(T)$ is relevant if, and only if, $w_ng$ is Jacquet-Ye relevant. Therefore, there exists a standard Levi subgroup $M$ of $G$, such that 
$$w_ng= a_Mw_l^M,$$
with $a_M$ an element of the center $Z_M$ of $M$, and $w_l^M$ is the longest element in $W_M=W_G\cap M$. Finally, an element $g\in N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}$ is of the form 
$$g= a_Mw_l^Mw_n.$$

label: n-root
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{n-root}
    Let $V$ be a unipotent group (defined over a field of characteristic $0$), and let $n\geq 1$ be an integer. Any element $v\in V$ admits a unique $n$-th root.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us show that the following morphism is bijective
    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
         & V & \longrightarrow & V \\
         & v & \longmapsto & v^n
    \end{array}.$$
    Since the exponential map provides an isomorphism, of algebraic varieties, between $V$ and its Lie algebra $\mathfrak{V}$ (Proposition 14.32, in \cite{Milne_2017}), and 
    $$\mathrm{exp}(X)^n = \mathrm{exp}(nX),$$
    for all $X\in \mathfrak{V}$, we obtain the following commuting diagram.
    $$\xymatrix{
     V \ar[r]^{(\cdot)^n} & V    \\
     \mathfrak{V} \ar[u]^{\mathrm{exp}} \ar[r]_{n\cdot} &  \mathfrak{V}\ar[u]_{\mathrm{exp}}
     }$$
    Since $n$ is invertible, the map $\mathfrak{V}\to \mathfrak{V}$ given by the multiplication by $n$ is bijective. Therefore, 
    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
         & V & \longrightarrow & V \\
         & v & \longmapsto & v^n
    \end{array}$$
    is a bijection, i.e. for all $v\in V$ there exists a unique element $x\in V$ such that
    $$v= x^n.$$

label: unipdecomp
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{unipdecomp}
    Let $V$ be a unipotent group (defined over a field of characteristic $0$), and $\iota\in \mathrm{Aut}(V)$ be an involution. Denote by 
    $$V^{\iota =1} =\{v\in V \mid  \iota(v)=v\},$$
    and 
    $$V^{\iota = -1}=\{v\in V \mid  \iota(v)=v^{-1}\}.$$
    Then 
    $$V=V^{\iota = 1}V^{\iota = -1}.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v\in V$, remark that $\iota(v)^{-1}v\in V^{\iota=-1}$, because
    $$\iota(\iota(v)^{-1}v)= v^{-1}\iota(v) = (\iota(v)^{-1}v)^{-1}.$$
    Thanks to Lemma \ref{n-root}, there exists $b\in V$, such that 
    $$b^2 = \iota(v)^{-1}v,$$
    and we have 
    $$\iota(b)^2 = (\iota(v)^{-1}v)^{-1} = b^{-2},$$
    by uniqueness of the square-root, we have $b\in V^{\iota=-1}$, and $v = \iota(v)b^2$. 
    Now, set $a = vb^{-1}$, we have 
    $$a = \iota(v) b$$
    and therefore 
    $$\iota(a) = vb^{-1} = a.$$
    For an arbitrary $v\in V$, we have obtained a factorization 
    $$v = ab, \ \mathrm{with} \ a\in V^{\iota=1}, \ b\in V^{\iota = -1}, $$
    which finishes the proof.

title: Lemma

title: Remark
body_md: Proposition 2.1 of \cite{Benoist1984} actually shows that Lemma \ref{n-root} is also true for $V^{\iota=-1}$, although it is not a unipotent group.

label: relUn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{relUn}
    We have $U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}} = U(n)\cap G_{\mathrm{rel}}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The inclusion $ U(n)\cap G_{\mathrm{rel}} \subset U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}} $ is straightforward, using the definitions $N'=N\cap U(n)$ and $\psi'= \psi\vert_{N'}$. 

    Let $x\in  U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}}$, and let 
    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
        \theta' :  & (N\times N)_x & \to & (N\times N)_x \\
         & (n_1, n_2) & \mapsto & (n_1^*, n_2^*)
    \end{array}$$
    be an involution, where $g^* = w_n{}^t(g^{-1})^cw_n$. Let $(n_1, n_2)\in (N\times N)_x$, the involution $\theta'$ is well defined, because 
    \begin{align*}
        (n_1^*)^{-1}xn_2^* & =  (w_n{}^tn_1^cw_n)x(w_n{}^t(n_2^{-1})^cw_n), 
    \end{align*}
    and $x\in U(n)$ implies that $w_nxw_n = ({}^tx^{-1})^c$, therefore
    \begin{align*}
        (n_1^*)^{-1}xn_2^* & =  w_n({}^tn_1{}^tx^{-1}{}^tn_2^{-1})^cw_n, \\
        & = w_n({}^t(n_1^{-1}xtn_2)^{-1})^cw_n, \\
        & = w_n {}^t(x^{-1})^cw_n, \\
        & = x^*, \\
        & = x.
    \end{align*}
    Applying Lemma \ref{unipdecomp} to $V= (N\times N)_x$ and $\iota = \theta'$, we obtain 
    $$(N\times N)_x = (N\times N)_x^{\theta'=1}(N\times N)_x^{\theta'=-1},$$
    where 
    $$(N\times N)_x^{\theta'=1} = \{(u_1, u_2)\in (N\times N)_x, \ \theta' (u_1, u_2) = (u_1, u_2) \},$$
    and 
    $$(N\times N)_x^{\theta'=-1} = \{(u_1, u_2)\in (N\times N)_x, \ \theta' (u_1, u_2) = (u_1, u_2)^{-1} = (u_1^{-1}, u_2^{-1})\}.$$
    In other words,
    $$(N\times N)_x^{\theta'=-1} = \{(u_1, u_2) \in (N\times N)_x, \ u_i^* = u_i^{-1} \}.$$
    By the definition of $\psi$, we have 
    $$\psi(u^*) = \psi(u).$$
    
    Denote by $N^{*=-1}$ the set of elements of $u\in N$ such that $u^*=u^{-1}$, and remark that 
    $$\psi(u)=\psi(u^*)=\psi(u)^{-1}, \ \mathrm{for \ all} \ u\in N^{*=-1},$$
    or equivalently 
    $$\psi^2\vert_{N^{*=-1}}\equiv 1, \ \mathrm{i.e.} \ \psi\vert_{N^{*=-1}}\equiv \pm 1.$$
    Let $u\in N^{*=-1}$, thanks to Lemma \ref{antiinv}, there exists $v\in N$, such that 
    $$u= (v^*)^{-1}v.$$
    Then 
    $$\psi(u) =\psi(v^*)^{-1}\psi(v) = 1, $$
    and therefore, 
    $$\psi\vert_{N^{*=-1}}\equiv 1.$$
    
    Finally, 
    $$(N\times N)_x^{\theta'=1} = \{(u_1, u_2) \in (N\times N)_x, \ u_i = u_i^* \} \cong (N'\times N')_x, $$
    and since $x\in  U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}}$, 
    $$\psi\boxtimes \psi^{-1}\vert_{(N\times N)_x^{\theta'=1}} = \psi'\boxtimes (\psi')^{-1}\vert_{(N'\times N')_x}\equiv 1.$$
    This shows that for $x\in U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}}$, we have 
    $$\psi\boxtimes \psi^{-1}\vert_{(N\times N)_x}\equiv 1,$$
    or equivalently $x\in U(n) \cap G_{\mathrm{rel}}$.

label: Srel1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Srel1}
    We have $S_{\mathrm{rel}} = S \cap G_{\mathrm{rel}}.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $s\in S$, recall that an element of $(N \times N)_s$ is of form $(u, sus^{-1})$, with $u\in N$, therefore we consider the following embedding
    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
         & N_s & \hookrightarrow & (N\times N)_s\\
         & u & \mapsto & (u, u^c)
    \end{array}.$$
    Let $\theta$ be the involution defined by 
    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
        \theta :  & (N\times N)_s & \to &  (N\times N)_s \\
         & (u_1, u_2) & \mapsto & (u_2^c, u_1^c)
    \end{array}.$$
    Indeed, $\theta$ preserves $(N\times N)_s$, as for $(u_1,u_2)\in (N\times N)_s$, we have 
    $$u_1^{-1}su_2 = s$$
    taking the conjugate and the inverse of this expression, we obtain 
    $$(u_2^c)^{-1}su_1^c = s,$$
    that is $(u_2^c, u_1^c)\in (N\times N)_s$. We apply Lemma \ref{unipdecomp} to $V = (N\times N)_s$ and $\iota = \theta$, we obtain
    $$(N\times N)_s = (N\times N)_s^{\theta=1}(N\times N)_s^{\theta=-1},$$
    where 
    $$(N\times N)_s^{\theta=1} = \{(u_1, u_2)\in (N\times N)_s, \ \theta (u_1, u_2) = (u_1, u_2) \},$$
    and 
    $$(N\times N)_s^{\theta=-1} = \{(u_1, u_2)\in (N\times N)_s, \ \theta (u_1, u_2) = (u_1, u_2)^{-1} = (u_1^{-1}, u_2^{-1})\}.$$
    In other words,
    $$(N\times N)_s^{\theta=-1} = \{(u_1, (u_1^c)^{-1}) \in N\times N \mid \ (u_1^c)^{-1} = su_1s^{-1}\}.$$
    For $(u_1,(u_1^c)^{-1})\in (N\times N)_s^{\theta=-1}$, we have 
    $$\psi(u_1)\psi((u_1^c)^{-1})^{-1} = \psi(u_1)\psi(u_1^c) = \psi(u_1)\psi(u_1)^{-1}=1.$$
    It implies that 
    $$\psi\boxtimes \psi^{-1}\vert_{(N\times N)_s} = \psi\boxtimes \psi^{-1}\vert_{(N\times N)_s^{\theta=1}}.$$
                                                                         
    Finally, 
    \begin{align*}
        (N\times N)_s^{\theta=1} & = \{(u, sus^{-1}) \in (N\times N)_s, \ u^c = sus^{-1}\} \cong N_s
        .
    \end{align*}
    Through this isomorphism, we obtain 
    $$\psi\boxtimes \psi^{-1}\vert_{(N\times N)_s^{\theta = 1}} = \psi\vert_{N_s}^2.$$
    If $s\in S_{\mathrm{rel}}$, we have 
    $$\psi\vert_{N_s} \equiv 1,$$
    and therefore
    $$\psi\boxtimes \psi^{-1}\vert_{(N\times N)_s^{\theta = 1}} \equiv 1.$$
    If $s\in S\cap G_{\mathrm{rel}}$, then
    $$\psi\boxtimes \psi^{-1}\vert_{(N\times N)_s^{\theta = 1}} = \psi\vert_{N_s}^2 \equiv 1.$$
    Since $N_s$ is a unipotent group, we apply Lemma \ref{n-root}, and we get that for all $u\in N_s$, there exists $v\in N_s$ such that $u=v^2$, that is 
    $$\psi(u) = \psi(v)^2 = 1.$$
    Therefore, 
    $$\psi\vert_{N_s} \equiv 1,$$
    meaning that $s\in S_{\mathrm{rel}}$.
    To conclude, we have shown that for all $s\in S$
    $$\psi\boxtimes \psi^{-1}\vert_{(N\times N)_s^{\theta = 1}} \equiv 1$$
    is equivalent to 
    $$\psi\vert_{N_s} \equiv 1,$$
    that is $S_{\mathrm{rel}} = S\cap G_{\mathrm{rel}}$.

label: relS2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{relS2}
    We have $S\cap G_{\mathrm{rel}} = (N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap S)\cdot N$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us first show that $N_G(T)\cap S$ is a system of representatives for the $N$-orbits in $S$. 

    First of all, we know that $N_G(T)$ is a system of representatives for the $N\times N$-orbits in $G$, thanks to the Bruhat decomposition. Under the embedding 
    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
     & S & \hookrightarrow & G \\
     & Hg & \mapsto & (g^c)^{-1}g 
    \end{array},$$
    for an element $s\in S$, we have 
    $$s\cdot N \subset NsN.$$
    Now, for all $g \in N_G(T)$, if $(NgN)\cap S\not = \emptyset$ then $g\in N_G(T)\cap S$. Indeed, let $g \in N_G(T)$, such that $(NgN)\cap S\not = \emptyset$. There exists $(n_1,n_2)\in N\times N$, such that 
    $$n_1^cg^cn_2^c = n_2^{-1}g^{-1}n_1^{-1}.$$
    In other words, 
    $$Ng^cN \cap Ng^{-1}N\not = \emptyset.$$
    Since $N_G(T)$ is a system of representatives for the $N\times N$-orbits in $G$, we obtain 
    $$Ng^cN = Ng^{-1}N,$$
    and therefore $g^c=g^{-1}$.

    
    It remains to show that for all $g\in N_G(T)$, $(NgN)\cap S$ contains at most one $N$-orbit in $S$. According to the previous observation, it suffices to show that for all $s\in S$, 
    $$NsN\cap S = s\cdot N.$$
    We use again the involution
    $$\begin{array}{cccc}
        \theta :  & N\times N & \to &  N\times N \\
         & (u_1, u_2) & \to & (u_2^c, u_1^c)
    \end{array}.$$
    We have 
    $$(N\times N)^{\theta= 1} = \{(u, u^c), u \in N\}.$$
    In other words, 
    $$NsN\cap S = s\cdot N$$
    is equivalent to 
    $$s\cdot (N\times N) \cap S = s\cdot (N\times N)^{\theta= 1}.$$
    Let $(u_1, u_2)\in N\times N$ such that $s\cdot (u_1,u_2)\in S$, we show that 
    $$(u_1,u_2)\in (N\times N)_s(N\times N)^{\theta =1}.$$
    We have 
    $$(s\cdot (u_1,u_2))^c = (s\cdot (u_1,u_2))^{-1}, $$
    hence 
    $$s^c\cdot (u_1^c,u_2^c) = s^{-1}\cdot (u_2,u_1),$$
    and then, since $s^c = s^{-1}$, 
    $$s\cdot (u_2^c,u_1^c) = s\cdot (u_1,u_2).$$
    This implies that 
    $$s^c\cdot ((u_1,u_2)\theta(u_1,u_2)^{-1}) = s,$$
    and therefore
    $$(u_1,u_2)\theta(u_1,u_2)^{-1} \in (N\times N)_s.$$
    We apply Lemma \ref{antiinv} to $V=(N\times N)_s$ and $\iota =\theta\vert_{(N\times N)_s}$. We have already shown that ${(N\times N)_s}$ is $\theta$-stable. The element $(u_1,u_2)\theta(u_1,u_2)^{-1} \in (N\times N)_s$, satifies
    $$\theta( (u_1,u_2)\theta(u_1,u_2)^{-1}) = \theta (u_1,u_2)(u_1,u_2)^{-1} = ( (u_1,u_2)\theta(u_1,u_2)^{-1})^{-1},$$
    that is $(u_1,u_2)\theta(u_1,u_2)^{-1} \in (N\times N)_s^{\theta =-1}$.
    Hence, there exists an element $v\in(N\times N)_s$, such that 
    $$(u_1,u_2)\theta(u_1,u_2)^{-1} = \theta(v)^{-1}v,$$
    or equivalently
    $$\theta(u_1,u_2) = v^{-1}\theta(v)(u_1,u_2).$$
    Set $x = \theta(v)(u_1,u_2)$, we have 
    $$\theta(x) = v\theta(u_1,u_2) = v(v^{-1}\theta(v)(u_1,u_2)) = \theta(v)(u_1,u_2) = x,$$
    therefore $x\in (N\times N)^{\theta =1}$, and 
    $$(u_1, u_2) = \theta(v)^{-1} x \in (N\times N)_s(N\times N)^{\theta =1}.$$
    So far we have shown that 
    $$s\cdot (N\times N) \cap S \subset s\cdot (N\times N)_s (N\times N)^{\theta= 1},$$
    but $s\cdot (N\times N)_s = s$, thus
    $$s\cdot (N\times N) \cap S \subset s\cdot (N\times N)^{\theta= 1}.$$
    Since the inverse inclusion is direct, we obtain
    $$s\cdot (N\times N) \cap S = s\cdot (N\times N)^{\theta= 1}.$$
    Combining the fact that 
    $$S = (N_G(T)\cap S) \cdot N$$
    with Lemma \ref{Srel1}, we conclude that 
    $$S\cap G_{\mathrm{rel}} = (N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap S)\cdot N. $$

title: Lemma
body_md:
We have 
    $$ N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap U(n) = N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap S.$$
    In particular,
    $$N'\backslash U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}}/N' \cong S_{\mathrm{rel}}/N.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that 
    $$N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap U(n) = \{n\in N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}, \ w_n{}^t(n^{-1})w_n = n^c \},$$
    and 
    $$N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap S = \{n\in N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}, \ n^{-1} = n^c \}.$$
    According to Remark \ref{Relelements}, an element $n\in N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}$ is of the form 
    $$n= a_Mw_l^Mw_n$$
    where $M$ is a Levi subgroup of $G$, $a_M$ is an element of the center $Z_M$ of $M$ and $w_l^M$ is the longest element in the Weyl group $W_M$ of $M$. Remark that 
    $$w_n{}^tnw_n = w_n(w_nw_l^Ma_M)w_n=a_Mw_l^Mw_n= n.$$
    If, moreover, $n\in N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap U(n)$, then 
    $$n = w_n{}^tnw_n = (n^{c})^{-1} \in  N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap S.$$ 
    Finally, if $n\in N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap S$, then 
    $$w_n{}^tn^{-1}w_n = n^{-1} = n^c,$$
    that is $n\in N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap U(n)$.
    Therefore, 
    $$ N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap U(n) = N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap S.$$
    Thanks to Lemma \ref{relUn}, we have 
    $$N'\backslash U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}}/N' \cong N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap U(n),$$
    that is, 
    $$N'\backslash U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}}/N' \cong N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap S.$$
    Lemma \ref{Srel1} and Lemma \ref{relS2}, provide
    $$S_{\mathrm{rel}}/N = S\cap G_{\mathrm{rel}}/N \cong N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap S,$$
    and therefore
    $$N'\backslash U(n)_{\mathrm{rel}}/N' \cong S_{\mathrm{rel}}/N.$$

title: Conjecture
body_md:
Two functions $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, and $f'\in C_c^\infty(U(n))$ are \emph{transfers} from one to the other, if and only if 
     $$ O_{\psi}(x, f)=O_{\psi'}(y,f'),$$
     for $ y = x \in N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap U(n) = N_G(T)_{\mathrm{rel}}\cap S$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
If two functions $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, and $f'\in C_c^\infty(U(n))$ are {transfers} from one to the other, then
     $$O_{\psi}(1,f)=O_{\psi'}(1,f').$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f\in C^\infty_c(G)$, recall that the orbital integral on the trivial class is given by
    $$O_\psi(1,f) = \int_{(H\times N)_1\backslash H\times N} f(h^{-1}u)\psi(u)dhdu.$$
    The stabilizer
    $$(H\times N)_1=\left\{(h,n)\in H\times N \vert \ h^{-1}n=1\right\}$$
    can be described as
    $$(H\times N)_1=\left\{(n,n)\in H\times N \vert \ n\in N\cap H\right\}\cong N\cap H.$$
    Therefore, 
    $$O_\psi(1,f) = \int_{(N\cap H)\backslash H} \int_{N}f(h^{-1}u)\psi(u)dudh.$$
    We have defined in Section \ref{WhittSection}, the following function
    $$W_{f, \pi}(g_1, g_2):= W_{f_\pi}(g_1, g_2)= \int_N^* f_\pi(g_1^{-1}ug_2)\psi_n(u)^{-1} du, \ (g_1,g_2)\in G\times G.$$
    Thanks to the Plancherel-Whittaker formula (see Proposition 2.142 in \cite{RBPPlanch}), we obtain
    $$O_\psi(1,f) = \int_{(N\cap H)\backslash H} \int_{\mathrm{Temp}(G)}W_{f, \pi}(h,1)d\mu_G(\pi)dh,$$
    where we use the same measure normalization as in \cite{RBPPlanch}.
    We then use Corollary 3.51 in \cite{RBPPlanch}, to write
    $$O_\psi(1,f) = \int_{\mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n))}\beta(W_{f, BC_n(\pi')}^1)d\mu_{U(n)}(\pi'),$$
    and thus, 
    $$O_\psi(1,f) = \int_{\mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n))}I_{BC_n(\pi')}(f)d\mu_{U(n)}(\pi').$$
    On the unitary side, we have $(N'\times N')_1 \cong N'$, therefore
    \begin{align*}
        O_{\psi'}(1,f') & =\int_{(N'\times N')_1\backslash N'\times N'} f'(n_1^{-1}n_2)\psi'(n_1n_2^{-1})dn_1dn_2, \\
        & = \int_{ N'} f'(n)\psi'(n)dn.
    \end{align*}
    Using again the Plancherel-Whittaker formula, Proposition 2.142 in \cite{RBPPlanch}, we get
    $$O_{\psi'}(1,f') = \int_{\mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n))}W_{f', \pi}(1,1)d\mu_{U(n)}(\pi),$$
    and therefore
    $$O_{\psi'}(1,f') = \int_{\mathrm{Temp_{gen}}(U(n))} J_{\pi}(f')d\mu_{U(n)}(\pi).$$

    Finally, if $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$ is the transfer of $f'\in C^\infty_c(U(n))$, then we have
    $$I_{BC_n(\pi)}(f) = J_\pi(f'),$$
    which, according to the previous calculations, implies 
    $$O_{\psi}(1,f) = O_{\psi'}(1,f').$$
